1. Spatial-temporal load prediction of electric bus charging station based on S2TAT
• Method: Synchronous Spatial-Temporal Attention Transformer (S2TAT). It incorporates an adaptive adjacency matrix for dynamic spatial dependency learning and a periodicity extraction mechanism.
• Node & Edge: Nodes represent charging stations; Edges represent the connectivity between them.
• Demand: The number of charging vehicles (electric buses) at a specific station in a specific period of time.
• Prediction: Charging load (number of vehicles) for electric buses.
• Data: Operational data from 321 new energy electric buses in Shanghai, converted into a charging load matrix and distance matrix.
2. Spatio-temporal forecasting of EV charging demand in urban communities considering differentiated user characteristics
• Method: A framework integrating a Temporal Graph Convolutional Network (T-GCN) for traffic flow, Maximum Entropy Estimation for Origin-Destination (O-D) analysis, Dynamic Traffic Assignment (DTA), and an enhanced M/M/C/K queuing model.
• Node & Edge: Nodes represent traffic nodes (intersections/endpoints) or charging station locations within the Transportation Network (TN); Edges represent road segments.
• Demand: Charging demand is derived from traffic flow and classified into fast charging (Type B, public stations) and slow charging (Type A, private/workplace).
• Prediction: Spatio-temporal EV charging demand.
• Data: Traffic flow data, temperature data, and road network topology from a city in East China.
3. Load probabilistic forecasting for electric vehicle charging station cluster: Adaptive multivariate spatiotemporal graph fusion technology
• Method: Adaptive Multivariate Spatiotemporal Graph (AMSTG) model. It combines a time Transformer, a multi-layer graph fusion module (dynamic and static graphs), and a Copula-based probabilistic decoder.
• Node & Edge: Nodes represent charging stations; Edges represent correlations between load attributes (intra-station) or spatial dependencies (inter-station).
• Demand: Multivariate demand consisting of charging power (kW) and charging station occupancy rate.
• Prediction: Probabilistic forecasting of charging load (power and occupancy).
• Data: Real-world data from 247 public EV charging stations in Shenzhen, China.
4. A Physics-Informed and Attention-Based Graph Learning Approach for Regional Electric Vehicle Charging Demand Prediction
• Method: Physics-Informed Attention-based Graph learning (PIAST / PAG). It uses a 2D-CNN for feature engineering, a spatio-temporal dual attention module (GAT and LSTM), and Physics-informed Meta-learning (PIML) to embed economic laws (Price Elasticity of Demand).
• Node & Edge: Nodes represent traffic zones/areas; Edges represent spatial adjacency (neighboring relationships).
• Demand: The number of EVs being serviced in a specific area (occupancy).
• Prediction: Regional EV charging demand (occupancy).
• Data: 18,061 EV charging piles in Shenzhen, China.
5. Privacy-preserving coordination of power and transportation networks using spatiotemporal GAT for predicting EV charging demands
• Method: Predict-Then-Optimize (PTO) framework using a Spatiotemporal Graph Attention Network (STGAT) combined with an enhanced M/M/C/N queuing model.
• Node & Edge: Nodes are sensor/traffic nodes in the Urban Transportation Network (UTN); Edges represent connectivity.
• Demand: EV charging demand derived from predicted vehicle flow.
• Prediction: Vehicle flow (traffic flow) converted to charging demand.
• Data: PeMSD4 traffic dataset (San Francisco) and IEEE 33-bus power system data.
6. An adaptive spatio-temporal graph recurrent network for short-term electric vehicle charging demand prediction

• Prediction: Short-term EV charging demand.

7. Citywide electric vehicle charging demand prediction approach considering urban region and dynamic influences

The provided sources explore advanced machine learning and deep learning frameworks designed to forecast electric vehicle (EV) charging demand and station occupancy. These methodologies frequently integrate spatio-temporal graph convolutional networks (GCN) and attention mechanisms to capture complex dependencies between historical usage, traffic flow, and geographical locations. Beyond core charging data, the models incorporate diverse external variables such as weather conditions, electricity pricing, and land-use characteristics to enhance predictive accuracy. Several studies also highlight the importance of data pre-processing and causal relationship modeling to address issues like missing data and network interdependencies. Ultimately, these research efforts aim to optimize grid stability, improve infrastructure planning, and support the large-scale integration of EVs into urban energy systems.

summarize the methodology for the Graph Networks for EV Charging Optimization and Prediction

The methodology for Graph Networks used in EV Charging Optimization and Prediction typically involves building complex architectures that integrate temporal and spatial modeling techniques, often augmented with attention mechanisms or specific physics/economic constraints to enhance accuracy and interpretability.
Key methodologies observed across various models include:
1. Core Architecture and Feature Extraction
Models generally employ a combination of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for spatial feature learning and various Recurrent/Convolutional architectures for temporal dynamics,.
• Spatial Modeling (GCN/GAT): Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN) or Graph Attention Networks (GAT) are applied to extract spatial features and dependencies between charging nodes,,,,,,,. This process captures local connectivity based on relationships like distance or traffic flow,. GAT, specifically, dynamically assigns attention weights to neighboring nodes, adapting to the influence strength of different stations,,.
• Temporal Modeling (LSTM/GRU/TCN/Transformer): Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) or Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) are commonly used to capture temporal correlations and dependencies within the load sequences, overcoming gradient issues common in simpler recurrent networks,,,,,,,. Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) are also employed, leveraging dilated causal convolution to expand the receptive field exponentially for modeling long-range temporal sequences efficiently,.
2. Handling Complex Spatial and Dynamic Relationships
To move beyond static geographic assumptions, several specialized techniques are integrated:
• Adaptive Graph Learning: Models like the Adaptive Spatial-Temporal Graph Recurrent Network (ASTGRN) and the Adaptive Multivariate Spatiotemporal Graph (AMSTG) dynamically learn spatial correlations from data, rather than relying solely on predefined distances,,,,. In ASTGRN, the adjacency matrix is derived from the pairwise similarity of evolving node embeddings,,.
• Multi-Graph Fusion: Architectures like the Multi-graph Attention Fusion Network (MGAT-MIC-LSTM) combine multiple relationship graphs (e.g., distance, traffic network, traffic density) to obtain a richer representation of spatial features,,,,,.
• Feature Integration for Graph Construction: The Traffic-Weather GCN (TW-GCN) uses both geographic proximity (Haversine distance) and demand similarity (Dynamic Time Warping, DTW) to construct heterogeneous adjacency matrices,. The AMSTG uses a fusion of dynamic (real-time feature-based) and static (embedding-based) graphs at intra-station and inter-station levels,.
3. Incorporating External Factors and Constraints
Prediction accuracy is often improved by integrating external factors beyond historical load:
• Multivariate Data Input: Models frequently incorporate external data such as charging price, station occupancy rate, weather conditions (temperature, humidity), points of interest (POIs), and date/holiday information,,,,,,,,.
• Synchronous Spatial-Temporal Modeling: The synchronous spatial-temporal attention transformer (S2TAT) model synchronously extracts spatial and temporal features, ensuring that their interdependencies are captured simultaneously rather than sequentially,,.
• Physics/Economic Constraints (PIAST): The Physics-Informed Graph Learning Approach (PIAST) incorporates a multi-step training strategy (pre-training, prompting, and fine-tuning) to embed knowledge derived from economic laws, such as the price elasticity of demand (PED), into the model. This makes the forecast results interpretable and adaptable to pricing strategies,,.
• Causality and Critical Node Focus (CADGN): The Causality-Aware Dynamic Multi-Graph Convolutional Network (CADGN) constructs a causality graph using the Time-Fragment Greedy Equivalence Search (TFGES) algorithm to model cause-and-effect relationships,. It also identifies "critical" nodes (influential charging stations) based on a centrality score derived from historical load dependencies to dynamically model their relationships,.
4. Optimization and Multi-step Prediction
Methodologies designed for practical application often include mechanisms for multi-step forecasting and outlier mitigation:
• Probabilistic Forecasting (AMSTG): The Adaptive Multivariate Spatiotemporal Graph (AMSTG) model uses a non-parametric Copula framework with Deep Sigmoid Flows (DSF) to model the joint distribution of variables, providing quantification of prediction uncertainty and handling missing data,,.
• Attention-based Output Refinement: S2TAT and G-STAN use attention-based aggregation mechanisms in their output modules to dynamically assign weights to inputs, helping to filter noise and amplify critical information, especially important for handling spatial heterogeneity,.
• Long-Term Forecasting: S2TAT leverages a non-local attention mechanism to effectively capture spatial-temporal features in long-term series (12 hours or more),.
Discuss what these sources say about Applications & Coordination, in the larger context of Advanced Techniques & Frameworks.

The adoption of advanced techniques and frameworks—such as various forms of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), attention mechanisms, and deep learning architectures—is fundamentally driven by the need to support critical applications, particularly those requiring complex coordination across energy and transportation systems.
Applications: Forecasting as a Foundation for Control
The central application identified across the sources is the accurate spatio-temporal forecasting of Electric Vehicle (EV) charging load, demand, or availability. This accurate prediction capacity serves as the indispensable foundation for advanced control and coordination tasks, ensuring effective resource allocation and maintaining system reliability. Models like the asynchronous spatial-temporal attention transformer (S2TAT) and the adaptive spatial-temporal graph recurrent network (ASTGRN) are developed explicitly to boost prediction accuracy by simultaneously modeling temporal and spatial dependencies.
Coordination of Coupled Networks (PDN and UTN)
Advanced modeling frameworks are essential for coordinating operations between the independent Power Distribution Networks (PDNs) and Urban Transportation Networks (UTNs).
• Predict-Then-Optimize (PTO) Framework: Because PDNs and UTNs are operated independently and information privacy must be maintained, a centralized joint optimization model is often unrealistic. The advanced solution is the PTO framework, where the PDN operator first uses a model like the Spatiotemporal Graph Attention Network (STGAT) to forecast EV charging demands based on UTN traffic flow data. These accurate forecasts are then integrated into a multi-period PDN scheduling model to achieve coordinated optimization while preserving privacy.
• Queuing and Traffic Flow Models: The STGAT model extracts dynamic spatial-temporal correlations from historical UTN traffic data, and these predicted traffic flows are converted into precise EV charging load predictions using an enhanced M/M/C/N queuing model. This integrated approach allows for system stability analysis, preventing overloads at charging stations and ensuring grid stability.
Coordination through Dynamic Pricing, Load Balancing, and Market Participation
Advanced techniques are directly applied to real-time operational coordination, particularly concerning financial incentives and load management.
• Dynamic Pricing and Interpretability: Models incorporating physics-informed knowledge, such as the Physics-informed and Attention-based Graph learning approach (PIAST), are used to assist in pricing strategies. PIAST utilizes Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) training to uncover the price elasticity of demand (PED) and model the spatial spillover effect of price adjustments on adjacent charging areas. This makes the model economically interpretable and directly supports pricing decision-making.
• Load Balancing via Reinforcement Learning (RL): A novel hybrid approach combines deep Q-learning (DQL) with Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) for dynamic load balancing and adaptive pricing in charging networks. This framework leverages a pre-trained GNN (like PAG) to predict demand elasticity and informs the RL agent on optimal price adjustments to minimize utilization variance and prevent station overloads.
• Energy Market Integration: Accurate forecasting is essential for EVCS aggregators to participate profitably in the energy market. Models like mRGC-CBi-LSTM forecast charging demand to enable aggregators to devise effective bidding strategies for the Day-Ahead Market (DAM) and Real-Time Market (RTM) under market rules, such as those of CAISO.
• Grid Constraint Compliance: The EGAT-LSTM prediction method is designed specifically to ensure forecasting accuracy during distribution network upgrades (including changes in topology structure and line renovation), which causes non-regression changes in node characteristics. By integrating edge aggregation information, the model extracts and learns line impedance changes to preserve effective prediction despite network alterations.
Advanced Applications for Strategic Planning
Advanced frameworks extend beyond real-time operations to support long-term strategic planning and infrastructure development.
• Infrastructure Allocation: GCNN-LSTM models are used to accurately predict long-term EV demand growth, which serves as the input for solving multi-objective optimization problems (e.g., Q-learning) to determine the optimal number and locations for allocating Charging Stations (CSs) and Distributed Generators (DGs) over extended time stages.
• Pattern Recognition and Facility Assignment: The Variational Spatiotemporal Factorized Graph Neural Network (VSTF-GNN) integrates prediction with unsupervised pattern recognition. By decomposing the data into latent spatial and temporal patterns, it generates information valuable for informing regular and real-time charging facility assignments.
• Citywide Planning: The proposed CityEVCP model utilizes attentive hypergraph networks and variable selection layers to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy in citywide EV charging demand prediction, supporting foundational smart strategies like infrastructure planning and smart power supply.
Discuss what these sources say about Advanced Techniques & Frameworks, in the larger context of EV Charging Demand Forecasting: Advanced Models and Factors.

The field of EV charging demand forecasting relies heavily on advanced techniques and frameworks to overcome challenges such as modeling dynamic spatial dependencies, handling complex temporal patterns, integrating heterogeneous external factors, and quantifying uncertainty. The sources detail several cutting-edge approaches, primarily driven by deep learning, spatial-temporal modeling, and adaptive mechanisms.
I. Foundational Spatiotemporal Deep Learning Architectures
Accurate forecasting requires capturing both Temporal Relationships (TR) and Spatial Relationships (SR), ideally in a synchronous manner, to avoid incomplete feature extraction. Advanced models typically integrate Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) with sophisticated recurrent or convolutional modules:
• Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs): These are fundamental tools for modeling SR, particularly essential because EV charging stations and road networks constitute complex non-Euclidean data structures that conventional Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) struggle to handle effectively.
• Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks (T-GCN / STGCN): These models combine GCNs (for spatial features) with recurrent networks like GRUs or LSTMs (for temporal dynamics). The Synchronous Spatial-Temporal Attention Transformer (S2TAT) is a highly advanced variant that incorporates graph convolution into the powerful Transformer architecture to achieve synchronous spatial-temporal relationship (STR) modeling, overcoming limitations of models restricted to local computations or asynchronous processing.
• Challenges of Fixed Graphs: Many traditional GNN/STGCN methods rely on a predefined, static adjacency matrix (often based on geographical distance), which struggles to capture the temporal heterogeneity and dynamic evolution of spatial relationships inherent in real-world charging behaviors.
II. Innovations in Graph Structure Modeling
To address the limitations of static graphs, advanced frameworks employ techniques to learn and adapt the spatial topology dynamically:
• Adaptive Graph Learning: The core idea is to derive an Adaptive Adjacency Matrix (AAM) directly from the spatial-temporal data, rather than relying on prior knowledge like fixed geographic distances. The Adaptive Spatial-Temporal Graph Recurrent Network (ASTGRN) explicitly demonstrated that relying on geographic location as prior knowledge may undermine model performance.
• Multi-Graph Fusion: Models leverage heterogeneous or multi-view graphs to capture different aspects of correlation simultaneously:
    ◦ Heterogeneous STGCN: Constructs a geographic graph (based on location distance) and a demand graph (based on time-series similarity, measured via Dynamic Time Warping (DTW)) to model spatial correlations comprehensively.
    ◦ Multi-Graph Attention (MGAT-MIC-LSTM): This approach fuses multiple manually constructed graphs—such as distance graph, traffic network graph, and traffic density graph—to describe the spatial relationships between charging station clusters, optimizing their fusion based on the mutual information between influencing factors.
    ◦ Adaptive Multivariate Spatiotemporal Graph (AMSTG): Integrates dynamic and static graphs at both intra-station and inter-station levels, optimizing weights dynamically for probabilistic forecasting.
• Causality-Aware Dynamic Multi-Graph Convolutional Network (CADGN): This framework explicitly addresses the distinction between correlation and causal relationships (e.g., load shifts caused by pricing or service interruption) using a Causality-Aware Graph Learning Module (CAGLM). It also features a Critical Relationship Graph Learning Module (CRGLM) which dynamically models the evolving connections among the most influential ("critical") EVCS nodes, enhancing robustness and insights.
III. Integration of Advanced Mechanisms
Advanced models enhance feature extraction and robustness by integrating contextual information and novel computational strategies:
• Multivariate Modeling: The capacity to model multiple related load attributes simultaneously significantly boosts prediction accuracy. For example, the AMSTG framework jointly models charging power and station occupancy. The mRGC-CBi-LSTM model uses a Mutual Adjacency Matrix (MAM) incorporating distance, correlation, user comfort, and exogenous factors (day-type tendency features).
• Transformer-Based Temporal Modules: The Transformer architecture is favored for its parallel computation capabilities and ability to capture long-range temporal features, often integrated via self-attention mechanisms or modules like Autoformer and Informer. Some models utilize Dilated Causal Convolution (TCN) layers to efficiently extract temporal dependencies over long sequences.
• Attention-Based Feature Refinement: Attention mechanisms are extensively used to prioritize relevant information. This includes Temporal Pattern Attention (TPA) to quantify the degree of influence of different time periods, and attention-based aggregation in the output layer of S2TAT to dynamically weight outputs and reduce the impact of anomalies.
IV. Frameworks for Interpretability, Robustness, and Planning
These advanced frameworks go beyond accuracy to improve practical application through transparency, handling of unknowns, and direct support for planning:
• Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs): The PIAST framework introduces Physics-informed Meta-learning (PIML) in the pre-training step to incorporate common knowledge, such as the price elasticity of demand (PED), thus mitigating prediction biases inherent in data-driven models and ensuring causal interpretability.
• Probabilistic Forecasting and Uncertainty Quantification: Moving beyond deterministic results, advanced frameworks provide a distribution of potential outcomes.
    ◦ Queuing Theory: Used alongside traffic models (e.g., enhanced M/M/C/N model) to determine the EV arrival rate and forecast charging load under constraints like charging station capacity and user behavior uncertainty (refusal to join/impatient departure).
    ◦ Copula-based Probabilistic Decoder: Explicitly models the joint distribution of multivariate load variables (power and occupancy) to quantify uncertainty and provide reliable confidence intervals.
• Transfer Learning and Distributed Training: To improve scalability and adapt models efficiently to new regions or sparse data:
    ◦ Federated Meta Learning-based GCN (FMGCN): Addresses data isolation and heterogeneity across different urban clients (cities) by accelerating convergence and creating highly adaptable global models.
    ◦ Adapter Architectures (BAM): Lightweight modules like the Bridged Attention Module (BAM) are inserted into pre-trained ST-GCNs to allow Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) on new city networks with limited data.

Accurate forecasting requires accounting for dynamic relationships and diverse external factors,.
Advanced Models in EV Charging Demand Forecasting
Advanced models frequently utilize deep learning architectures, particularly Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) combined with attention mechanisms or recurrent units, to simultaneously capture temporal (TR) and spatial (SR) dependencies, known collectively as Spatio-Temporal Relationships (STR),.
1. Synchronous and Adaptive Graph Models (e.g., S2TAT, ASTGRN):
Several models emphasize dynamic and synchronous modeling of STR:
• The Synchronous Spatial-Temporal Attention Transformer (S2TAT) model explicitly addresses the limitations of asynchronous modeling by capturing temporal and spatial dependencies simultaneously,,. S2TAT uses a non-local attention mechanism to effectively model long-term spatial-temporal dependencies, defined as periods of 12 hours or more,.
• It improves accuracy by using an adaptive adjacency matrix instead of predefined graph structures, allowing dynamic learning of complex spatial dependencies in multi-station scenarios,,,.
• S2TAT handles the heterogeneity in spatial-temporal data (such as uneven demand across regions) via a time-wise graph convolution module, which assigns a unique convolution kernel to each time step,,.
• The Adaptive Spatial-Temporal Graph Recurrent Network (ASTGRN) uses an adaptive graph learning layer to dynamically capture spatial correlations, thus avoiding reliance on potentially inaccurate prior knowledge like geographic distance,. It integrates a graph convolutional kernel with Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) to form a graph recurrent layer for comprehensive spatial and temporal extraction,.
2. Multivariate and Probabilistic Models (e.g., AMSTG, VSTF-GNN):
To manage prediction uncertainty and utilize comprehensive data inputs, certain models focus on multivariate learning and probability distribution:
• The Adaptive Multivariate Spatiotemporal Graph (AMSTG) model proposes a multivariate learning framework that explicitly combines charging power and station occupancy rate,. This design captures the nonlinear coupling between power fluctuations and charger usage.
• For probabilistic output, AMSTG utilizes a Copula-based decoder with Deep Sigmoid Flows to explicitly model the joint probability distribution of multivariate load variables, providing reliable uncertainty quantification,.
• The Variational Spatiotemporal Factorized Graph Neural Network (VSTF-GNN) also integrates probabilistic inference by defining spatial patterns through a variational Bayesian method to capture uncertainty stemming from missing values,. It unifies prediction and pattern recognition by predicting future usage conditions as the product of a spatial pattern matrix and a temporal pattern matrix,.
3. Integrating External and Causal Factors (e.g., G-STAN, PIAST):
Models focusing on policy responsiveness and deep causal understanding integrate specific external factors into their core architecture:
• The Graph-based Spatio-Temporal Attention Network (G-STAN) integrates graph convolution and attention mechanisms and constructs a hybrid adjacency matrix that includes node attributes, spatial embedding (via Node2Vec), and dynamic weights, enhancing its adaptability to policy responses,,.
• G-STAN incorporates a Temporal Pattern Attention (TPA) module designed to dynamically assign importance weights, focusing on critical periods like peak hours and key functional areas,.
• The Physics-Informed Attention-Based Graph Learning (PIAST) approach uses an Attention-based GNN and introduces a Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) training module,. This approach guides the model to learn economic laws, such as the price elasticity of demand (PED), to prevent misinterpretation of price-demand relationships,,,.

Discuss what these sources say about Key Influencing Factors, in the larger context of EV Charging Demand Forecasting: Advanced Models and Factors.

The comprehensive analysis of EV charging demand forecasting highlights that accurate prediction relies on modeling an intricate interplay of temporal, spatial, behavioral, and external factors. Advanced forecasting models, particularly those leveraging Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and attention mechanisms, focus on integrating these diverse features to capture the complex spatio-temporal dependencies inherent in EV charging load dynamics.
The key influencing factors can be categorized based on whether they represent inherent dynamics of the charging load (temporal and spatial characteristics) or exogenous drivers (external conditions and socioeconomic context).
I. Inherent Charging Dynamics
A. Temporal Dependencies and Periodicity
Temporal features are fundamental to forecasting, as charging events are characterized by predictable cycles and fluctuations.
1. Periodicity: Charging load exhibits strong, regular periodic trends, such as daily or weekly charging peaks. These predictable cycles are instrumental in accurate modeling over time.
2. Short- and Long-Term Fluctuations: Models must distinguish between long-term trends (e.g., seasonal changes or regular daily routines) and short-term fluctuations (e.g., rapid charging events or congestion). Capturing these requires multi-scale temporal feature extraction, often spanning hourly, daily, and weekly segments.
B. Spatial Heterogeneity and Interdependence
Spatial factors define how the demand in one location is correlated with its neighbors, a critical consideration for models handling multi-station scenarios.
1. Inter-Station Correlation: Charging loads are highly interrelated across different stations, requiring modeling of their spatial correlation. This interdependence means that prediction must account for spillover effects when loads shift between adjacent areas.
2. Beyond Distance: Spatial dependencies are complex and are not solely based on geographic distance. Functional characteristics, such as distinguishing commercial areas from residential areas, are necessary to capture similarities in demand patterns, even if the stations are geographically distant.
3. Adaptive Topology: Since actual relationships between stations can evolve over time (dynamic correlation), advanced models employ adaptive or multi-graph structures (e.g., distance graph, traffic network graph, traffic density graph, or correlation graphs) rather than relying on a single predefined static adjacency matrix.
II. Exogenous and Contextual Drivers
Exogenous factors provide contextual information that dictates user behavior, price sensitivity, and environmental impact on charging demand.
A. Economic and Policy Factors
1. Electricity Price: The real-time electricity price or charging price is a dominant factor influencing user behavior and load profiles, particularly in liberalized markets. Accurate prediction models must assess the price elasticity of demand (PED) to ensure interpretability and support optimized dynamic pricing strategies.
2. Day-Type Tendency: Exogenous factors like public holidays and the day of the week (weekdays versus weekends) significantly influence travel purpose and user demand.
B. Vehicle State and User Behavior
1. Vehicle Parameters: The Initial State of Charge (SOC) and end SOC are crucial determinants of whether an EV driver chooses to charge, influencing the urgency and duration of the session.
2. User Preference and Uncertainty: Models must account for user characteristics (e.g., differentiating private cars from commercial fleets like taxis) and behavioral uncertainties, such as users who refuse to join the queue or depart impatiently due to long wait times.
3. Operational Status: The charging station occupancy rate directly reflects the current utilization and operational constraints, serving as a critical feature input for forecasting.
C. Environmental and Traffic Factors
1. Weather Conditions: Meteorological variables, including temperature, humidity, and precipitation, affect EV battery performance, user travel intentions, and overall charging demand.
2. Traffic Conditions: Real-time traffic flow, speed, and congestion are highly correlated with EV load, as they dictate vehicle arrival times and energy consumption. These factors are often integrated via TMCs (Traffic Message Channels) or road network data.
D. Static Socioeconomic Context
Long-term planning benefits from static urban characteristics, which are often integrated using Points of Interest (POIs) or aggregated demographic data.
1. Urban Form: Factors like land use mix, charging station density, and road network density are recognized as highly influential, defining the structural context that shapes long-term demand.
2. Socioeconomic Metrics: Population density and other socioeconomic indicators are used to contextualize charging behavior, linking consumption patterns to demographic realities.
Discuss what these sources say about Data/Feature Preprocessing, in the larger context of Advanced Techniques & Frameworks.

The sources emphasize that Data/Feature Preprocessing is a multifaceted and critical initial step for advanced techniques and frameworks in EV charging demand forecasting, moving far beyond simple normalization to include complex operations like dynamic data handling, imputation, feature engineering, and graph construction.
Here is a discussion of the roles and specific methodologies of data/feature preprocessing used:
1. Handling Time-Series Data Issues
Advanced methods rely on cleaning and structuring complex, often incomplete, time-series inputs to maximize predictive signal extraction.
• Data Cleaning and Outlier Management: Raw data frequently contains anomalies and missing values due to equipment malfunctions or irregular collection schedules. Simple linear interpolation is often applied to handle missing values, particularly in traffic flow data, to ensure the continuity required for training deep learning models. Outlier elimination can be performed using methods like the 3-sigma distribution method to detect anomalous data points.
• Resampling and Temporal Aggregation: Raw data collected at fine intervals (e.g., 5, 10, or 20 seconds) are commonly resampled or aggregated to lower frequencies (e.g., hourly intervals) to align the data with the prediction task and reduce dataset size. For instance, raw charging session data might be aggregated into an hourly time series representing total load demand or average charging load per hour.
• Normalization/Standardization: To ensure features contribute equally and to accelerate model convergence, observed load values and attributes are scaled. Min–Max normalization (scaling to a range like) and Z-score standardization (achieving zero mean and unit variance) are frequently used across different features, including load, price, and static attributes.
2. Feature Engineering and External Data Integration
Advanced models incorporate heterogeneous inputs to capture comprehensive spatio-temporal dependencies.
• Multivariate Input Construction: Models integrate various external factors into the input feature matrix, such as charging price, weather conditions (temperature, humidity, precipitation), time-related features (day-of-week, holiday status), and local infrastructure attributes (e.g., number of chargers, POIs).
• Feature Selection: To manage complexity and improve accuracy, statistical methods are used to filter inputs. For example, the Maximum Information Coefficient (MIC) is applied to quantify the correlation between charging load and various influencing factors, ensuring that only variables with strong correlation (e.g., typical day, electricity price, previous day load) are included in the model input.
• Periodic Feature Extraction: To capture the underlying cyclical behavior of charging demand (e.g., daily or weekly peaks), specialized extraction methods are used. The synchronous spatial-temporal attention transformer (S2TAT) model specifically incorporates a mechanism for processing periodic trends (e.g., daily and weekly cycles) beyond simple linear time slices. This involves reconstructing the sequence using historical data corresponding to similar periodic segments, like the load from the day before or the week before.
3. Graph Structure Construction and Refinement
The most significant aspect of preprocessing for GNN-based frameworks is defining the graph structure (adjacency matrix), which often involves transforming non-Euclidean relationships.
• Heterogeneous Graph Construction: To represent complex spatial correlations accurately, multiple graphs are often combined or defined based on specific criteria beyond simple geographic distance. Examples include constructing a geographic graph (based on Haversine distance) and a demand graph (based on time-series similarity measured via Dynamic Time Warping, DTW). Other multi-graph approaches fuse a distance graph, a traffic network graph, and a traffic density graph to capture richer topology.
• Dynamic and Adaptive Graph Learning: Recognizing that spatial relationships evolve dynamically, frameworks like ASTGRN and AMSTG employ adaptive graph learning where the adjacency matrix is derived dynamically from evolving node embeddings rather than relying solely on fixed geographical constraints. This is crucial because reliance on static geographic locations as prior knowledge may undermine model performance. In some models, the graph is constructed by a weighted combination of dynamic (data-driven) and static (predefined/embedding-based) graphs at both intra-station (attribute correlation) and inter-station (spatial correlation) levels.
• Embedding for Graph Construction: For models integrating Points of Interest (POIs), preprocessing includes using POI density or categorization to quantify functional similarity between regions. This involves embedding POI data into a feature vector and using similarity (like Pearson correlation) to define the adjacency matrix. Additionally, techniques like Node2Vec can be used to embed the nodes of the region graph, enhancing the representation of spatial topological relationships.
4. Preparation for Training and Evaluation
Finally, the processed data must be split and prepared according to the requirements of deep learning training protocols.
• Data Partitioning: Datasets are typically split chronologically into training, validation, and test sets, often with ratios like 6:2:2 or 7:1:2, to ensure that prediction is always conducted on unseen future data.
• Input Sequence Generation: The sliding window technique is applied to generate sequences of historical input data and corresponding future target data, defining the prediction horizon (e.g., using the past 12 hours to predict the next 3, 6, or 12 hours).
Discuss what these sources say about Training Optimization/Efficiency, in the larger context of Advanced Techniques & Frameworks.

The application of advanced techniques and frameworks for EV charging prediction places a strong emphasis on optimizing training and computational efficiency to ensure models are accurate, reliable, and deployable in real-time, resource-constrained environments. These optimization efforts span novel training strategies, architectural design improvements, and specific technical implementations.
I. Leveraging Advanced Training Strategies
Advanced frameworks frequently incorporate multi-step training protocols and distributed learning mechanisms to accelerate convergence and enhance model interpretability:
• Physics-Informed Meta-Learning (PIML): The Physics-Informed Attention-based Graph Learning approach (PIAST) employs a structured, three-step training process (pre-training, prompting, and fine-tuning) designed for efficiency and interpretability,. By embedding domain knowledge (like price elasticity of demand) early on, the final stage uses only prediction loss (L 
D
​
 ) on a limited set of parameters, allowing for highly efficient fine-tuning,,. This process demonstrated acceleration compared to related meta-learning models.
• Federated Meta-Learning (FMGCN): This framework integrates federated learning and meta-learning to tackle challenges arising from data heterogeneity (non-IID data) across multiple cities,. The mechanism pre-trains a global meta-model with strong generalization capabilities, enabling rapid local adaptation. This distributed pretraining mechanism significantly accelerated convergence, reducing the necessary training rounds by an average of over 62% compared to traditional federated learning benchmarks,,.
• Deep Q-Learning (DQL) Stability: For optimization tasks like dynamic load balancing, DQL frameworks enhance stability by utilizing techniques such as experience replay (which samples past experiences randomly to break the correlation between updates) and stable target networks that are updated less frequently,,. The training goal is optimized by configuring a reward function that encourages minimizing utilization variance and overload penalties,.
II. Optimizing Model Architecture for Speed and Resource Efficiency
Architectural designs are tailored to handle large volumes of spatial-temporal data quickly, focusing on parallel processing and reduced computational overhead.
• Parallelization and Sequence Handling: The Transformer architecture is often prioritized for its ability to handle data sequences in parallel, dramatically reducing training time compared to sequential recurrent approaches like LSTM. Models such as the Synchronous Spatial-Temporal Attention Transformer (S2TAT) achieve significant time efficiency by using an efficient parallel processing framework during both training and inference.
• Exponential Receptive Fields: Models designed to handle long sequence prediction efficiently, such as Graph WaveNet, adopt stacked dilated causal convolutions for the temporal component. This technique allows the receptive field size to grow exponentially rather than linearly, enabling the model to capture long-range temporal dependencies effectively while maintaining computational efficiency,,.
• Lightweight Inference and Deployment: Efficiency is critical for real-time application. The synchronous spatial-temporal graph transformer (S2TAT) proved capable of reducing computational complexity when predicting long-term series. Similarly, the Graph-based Spatio-Temporal Attention Network (G-STAN) boasts a lightweight design (0.27 M parameters) and achieved a fast real-time inference latency of 1.39 seconds, significantly faster than comparable STGCN and ST-ResNet models,.
• Dynamic and Multi-Graph Architectures: Using adaptive graph learning (e.g., in AGCRN and ASTGRN) eliminates reliance on rigid, predetermined graph adjacency matrices, simplifying the modeling of complex spatial dependencies,. The complexity of graph convolution operations depends on the number of nodes (N) and edges (∣E∣), often expressed as O(K⋅∣E∣⋅d). By modeling dynamic relationships through data-driven means, models avoid the excessive computational complexity that arises from forcing intricate long-term relationships onto simplified fixed-graph structures.
• Parallel Feature Fusion: The mutual residual graph convolution-combined bidirectional LSTM (mRGC-CBi-LSTM) framework uses a parallel structure to concatenate its spatial (mRGCN) and temporal (CBi-LSTM) feature extraction modules,. This is designed to preserve the integrity of both spatial and temporal dependencies, reducing information loss and interference often encountered in sequential processing architectures,.
III. Training Techniques and Metrics
Standardization of training techniques ensures robustness and fair comparisons:
• Common Optimization Practices: The Adam optimizer is the prevailing choice for training almost all advanced models (including ASTGRN, AMSTG, and G-STAN),,,. Training is typically governed by setting an initial learning rate (often 0.001), a batch size (often 32 or 64), and utilizing early stopping criteria based on validation performance to prevent overfitting,.
• Adaptive Transfer Learning: Custom transfer learning adapters like the Bridged Attention Module (BAM) are developed to minimize the parameters that require retraining during fine-tuning on new data sets. In experiments, BAM used only 3.02% of the total model parameters as trainable, showcasing efficiency while maintaining competitive predictive performance,.
• Evaluation Criteria: While Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) remain standard metrics for quantifying prediction precision,, advanced probabilistic models utilize metrics like the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS) to evaluate the reliability and sharpness of their prediction distribution (uncertainty quantification).

Based on the provided sources, here is the summary of the methodology, network structure (node/edge), demand definition, prediction target, and data used for each paper.
1. Spatial-temporal load prediction of electric bus charging station based on S2TAT
• Method: Synchronous Spatial-Temporal Attention Transformer (S2TAT). It incorporates an adaptive adjacency matrix for dynamic spatial dependency learning and a periodicity extraction mechanism.
• Node & Edge: Nodes represent charging stations; Edges represent the connectivity between them.
• Demand: The number of charging vehicles (electric buses) at a specific station in a specific period of time.
• Prediction: Charging load (number of vehicles) for electric buses.
• Data: Operational data from 321 new energy electric buses in Shanghai, converted into a charging load matrix and distance matrix.
2. Spatio-temporal forecasting of EV charging demand in urban communities considering differentiated user characteristics
• Method: A framework integrating a Temporal Graph Convolutional Network (T-GCN) for traffic flow, Maximum Entropy Estimation for Origin-Destination (O-D) analysis, Dynamic Traffic Assignment (DTA), and an enhanced M/M/C/K queuing model.
• Node & Edge: Nodes represent traffic nodes (intersections/endpoints) or charging station locations within the Transportation Network (TN); Edges represent road segments.
• Demand: Charging demand is derived from traffic flow and classified into fast charging (Type B, public stations) and slow charging (Type A, private/workplace).
• Prediction: Spatio-temporal EV charging demand.
• Data: Traffic flow data, temperature data, and road network topology from a city in East China.
3. Load probabilistic forecasting for electric vehicle charging station cluster: Adaptive multivariate spatiotemporal graph fusion technology
• Method: Adaptive Multivariate Spatiotemporal Graph (AMSTG) model. It combines a time Transformer, a multi-layer graph fusion module (dynamic and static graphs), and a Copula-based probabilistic decoder.
• Node & Edge: Nodes represent charging stations; Edges represent correlations between load attributes (intra-station) or spatial dependencies (inter-station).
• Demand: Multivariate demand consisting of charging power (kW) and charging station occupancy rate.
• Prediction: Probabilistic forecasting of charging load (power and occupancy).
• Data: Real-world data from 247 public EV charging stations in Shenzhen, China.
4. A Physics-Informed and Attention-Based Graph Learning Approach for Regional Electric Vehicle Charging Demand Prediction
• Method: Physics-Informed Attention-based Graph learning (PIAST / PAG). It uses a 2D-CNN for feature engineering, a spatio-temporal dual attention module (GAT and LSTM), and Physics-informed Meta-learning (PIML) to embed economic laws (Price Elasticity of Demand).
• Node & Edge: Nodes represent traffic zones/areas; Edges represent spatial adjacency (neighboring relationships).
• Demand: The number of EVs being serviced in a specific area (occupancy).
• Prediction: Regional EV charging demand (occupancy).
• Data: 18,061 EV charging piles in Shenzhen, China.
5. Privacy-preserving coordination of power and transportation networks using spatiotemporal GAT for predicting EV charging demands
• Method: Predict-Then-Optimize (PTO) framework using a Spatiotemporal Graph Attention Network (STGAT) combined with an enhanced M/M/C/N queuing model.
• Node & Edge: Nodes are sensor/traffic nodes in the Urban Transportation Network (UTN); Edges represent connectivity.
• Demand: EV charging demand derived from predicted vehicle flow.
• Prediction: Vehicle flow (traffic flow) converted to charging demand.
• Data: PeMSD4 traffic dataset (San Francisco) and IEEE 33-bus power system data.
6. An adaptive spatio-temporal graph recurrent network for short-term electric vehicle charging demand prediction
• Method: Adaptive Spatial-Temporal Graph Recurrent Network (ASTGRN). It uses an adaptive graph learning layer (data-driven adjacency matrix) and a graph recurrent layer (GCN + GRU).
• Node & Edge: Nodes represent charging stations; Edges represent spatial correlations learned via dynamic node embeddings (adaptive adjacency).
• Demand: The number of served EVs at a charging station.
• Prediction: Short-term EV charging demand.
• Data: Real-world EV GPS trajectory dataset of 76,774 private EVs and 1,128 charging stations in Beijing, China.
7. Citywide electric vehicle charging demand prediction approach considering urban region and dynamic influences
• Method: CityEVCP. Uses attentive hypergraph networks (clustering areas by POI), Graph Attention Network (GAT) for adjacency, a Variable Selection Network, and an improved Transformer encoder.
• Node & Edge: Nodes are travel communities/sub-areas; Edges are spatial neighbors (GAT) and hyperedges representing groups of areas with similar land-use attributes.
• Demand: Number of EV charging piles occupied (occupancy).
• Prediction: Citywide EV charging demand (occupancy).
• Data: ST-EVCDP dataset containing 18,061 public charging piles in Shenzhen, China.
8. Probabilistic prediction of electric vehicle load in service area incorporating highway spatiotemporal traffic information
• Method: TCN-GAT (Temporal Convolutional Network + Graph Attention Network) for traffic flow prediction, followed by a refined EV entry rate estimation and an improved queuing theory model.
• Node & Edge: Nodes are monitoring nodes (road sensors); Edges represent highway connections.
• Demand: EV charging load (calculated from traffic flow, entry probability, and service rates).
• Prediction: Highway traffic flow quantiles, converted to EV load.
• Data: England highway traffic flow dataset and highway driving data from Guizhou Province.
9. Variational spatiotemporal factorized graph neural networks for integrated electric vehicle usage prediction and pattern recognition...
• Method: Variational Spatiotemporal Factorized Graph Neural Network (VSTF-GNN). It decomposes data into spatial and temporal pattern matrices using a variational Bayesian method to handle missing data. It integrates STGNNs (STGCN, DCRNN, or AGCRN).
• Node & Edge: Nodes are detectors (freeway) or Traffic Analysis Zones (urban); Edges are flow-based (freeway) or distance-based (urban).
• Demand: EV flow (freeway) or charging occupancy (urban).
• Prediction: Regional EV usage patterns and future values.
• Data: FreewayEV dataset (Zhejiang, China) and UrbanEV dataset (Shenzhen, China).
10. Predicting electric vehicle charging demand using a heterogeneous spatio-temporal graph convolutional network
• Method: Heterogeneous Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Network. It constructs two graphs (geographic and demand) and uses GCN and GRU with a region-specific prediction module.
• Node & Edge: Nodes are charging regions; Edges represent geographic adjacency and demand similarity (via Dynamic Time Warping).
• Demand: Number of EVs served within a time interval and region.
• Prediction: Short-term EV charging demand.
• Data: GPS trajectory dataset of over 76,000 private EVs in Beijing, China.
11. Charging station cluster load prediction: Spatiotemporal multi-graph fusion technology
• Method: MGAT-MIC-LSTM (Multi-Graph Attention Fusion Network). Fuses multiple graphs (distance, traffic network, traffic density) and feature graphs (via Maximum Information Coefficient) using attention mechanisms and LSTM.
• Node & Edge: Nodes are charging stations or feature variables; Edges represent relationships (distance, traffic flow, correlation).
• Demand: Power load.
• Prediction: Charging station cluster load.
• Data: 10 EV charging stations in Xi’an, China.
12. Modeling of machine learning with SHAP approach for electric vehicle charging station choice behavior prediction
• Method: Machine Learning classifiers (Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes, Random Forest, XGBoost) combined with SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations) for interpretability.
• Node & Edge: Not applicable (Not a graph-based method).
• Demand: Charging station choice behavior (Fast vs. Normal charging).
• Prediction: Charging station choice class (Classification).
• Data: Real-world charging event data from 500 EVs in Japan.
13. An electric vehicle charging demand prediction approach based on a Graph-based Spatio-temporal Attention Network
• Method: Graph-based Spatio-Temporal Attention Network (G-STAN). Utilizes Residual Temporal Convolution Network (Res-TCN), Simple Graph Convolution Attention (Sim-GCA), and Temporal Pattern Attention (TPA).
• Node & Edge: Nodes are traffic zones; Edges are spatial connections.
• Demand: Charging demand (occupied charging piles).
• Prediction: Charging demand.
• Data: 18,061 charging piles in 247 traffic zones in Shenzhen, China.
14. Deep Spatio-Temporal Forecasting of Electrical Vehicle Charging Demand
• Method: Temporal Graph Convolutional Network (T-GCN). Combines GCN for spatial and LSTM for temporal modeling.
• Node & Edge: Nodes are charging stations; Edges are based on Haversine distance (thresholded).
• Demand: Daily energy demand (consumption).
• Prediction: Daily energy demand.
• Data: Publicly available charging transaction data from Palo Alto, USA.
15. Spatiotemporal Prediction of Electric Vehicle Charging Load Based on Large Language Models
• Method: EV-LLM. Integrates Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN) with a fine-tuned Large Language Model (LLAMA2) using a multimodal feature fusion module.
• Node & Edge: Nodes are EV charging stations; Edges represent correlations/adjacency.
• Demand: Charging load (power).
• Prediction: EV charging load.
• Data: Charging data from 10 stations in Palo Alto, California.
16. Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks for EV Charging Demand Forecasting Using Real-World Multi-Modal Data Integration
• Method: Traffic-Weather Graph Convolutional Network (TW-GCN). Uses a stacked GCN architecture with temporal components (1DCNN/LSTM/GRU/RNN) and K-means clustering.

• Demand: Energy consumption (kWh).
• Prediction: EV charging demand (energy consumption).
• Data: ChargePoint dataset (86 stations) in Tennessee, USA, plus traffic and weather data.
17. FMGCN: Federated Meta Learning-Augmented Graph Convolutional Network for EV Charging Demand Forecasting
• Method: Federated Meta Learning-based Graph Convolutional Network (FMGCN). Uses a GCN with spatiotemporal attention (GCNSA) backbone within a Federated Learning (FedAvg) and Meta-Learning (FOMAML) framework.
• Node & Edge: Nodes are urban regions/districts; Edges are neighboring relationships.
• Demand: Charging demand (aggregated from records).
• Prediction: Regional EV charging demand.
• Data: 25,246 EV charging piles across six cities in the Greater Bay Area, China.
18. Forecasting EV Charging Station Occupancy Using ST-GCN And Adapter-Based Transfer Learning
• Method: Spatio-Temporal Graph Convolutional Network (ST-GCN) using a Transformer for the temporal component. Introduces a Bridged Attention Module (BAM) adapter for transfer learning.
• Node & Edge: Nodes are charging stations; Edges are connections in a fully connected network (simplified for transfer).
• Demand: Occupancy (ratio of occupied chargers to total chargers).
• Prediction: Charging station occupancy.
• Data: ChargeFinder data for Sweden (Värnamo, Varberg, Malmö).
19. Graph WaveNet for Deep Spatial-Temporal Graph Modeling
• Method: Graph WaveNet. Uses a self-adaptive adjacency matrix (learned through node embeddings) and stacked dilated 1D convolutions.
• Node & Edge: Nodes are sensors; Edges are adaptive/learned dependencies.
• Demand: Traffic speed (used as a proxy for demand modeling in this context).

whatn I am talking about shoort time prediction it means in what time prediction?

In the context of electric vehicle (EV) charging demand forecasting, short-term prediction generally refers to forecasting horizons ranging from a few minutes to 24 hours, which are primarily used for real-time scheduling, dynamic pricing, and grid load management.
Based on the provided sources, short-term prediction is defined by the following specific timeframes:
• Sub-hourly to Hourly: Many advanced models focus on predicting demand for the next 15, 30, 45, or 60 minutes,,,. Other studies define short-term prediction simply as hourly forecasting,,.
• Multi-Hour: Some definitions specify a range of 1 to 5 hours or 3 to 6 hours. For instance, certain studies explicitly define their short-term prediction task as forecasting the next 3 hours,.
• Day-Ahead (24 Hours): In some contexts, short-term prediction extends to the next 24 hours (often broken down into 15-minute or hourly intervals) to support daily grid operation and market bidding,.
This is distinct from long-term prediction (e.g., yearly), which is typically used for infrastructure planning and urban development.

Comprehensive Summary of EV Charging Demand Forecasting Literature
1. Research Domain Overview
Your document collection addresses a critical challenge in sustainable transportation: accurate prediction of electric vehicle charging demand to support grid management, infrastructure planning, and charging station operations. The papers span from classical time-series methods to cutting-edge GNN architectures with advanced features like attention mechanisms, federated learning, and physics-informed constraints.

2. Demand Definition Heterogeneity
A key finding across the literature is the inconsistency in how "demand" is operationalized:

3. Core Methodological Approaches
3.1 Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs)

Spectral-based approaches: Using Chebyshev polynomial approximations to perform graph convolutions efficiently
Spatial-based approaches: Direct aggregation of neighborhood information

3.2 Graph Attention Networks (GATs)

Dynamically learn attention weights between nodes
Multi-head attention mechanisms for capturing diverse spatial relationships
Papers: STGAT, GAT-Autoformer, MSSTGAN

3.3 Advanced/Hybrid Architectures
ArchitectureKey InnovationAGCRNAdaptive graph learning without predefined adjacencyGraph WaveNetSelf-adaptive adjacency matrix + dilated causal convolutionsDCRNNDiffusion convolution with bidirectional graph propagationSTGCNStacked spatiotemporal blocks with gated temporal convolutionASTGCNSpatial + temporal attention mechanisms
3.4 Emerging Approaches

Physics-Informed GNNs (PAG/PIAST): Embed economic laws like price elasticity of demand
Federated Meta-Learning (FMGCN): Privacy-preserving distributed learning
LLM-based Methods (ChatEV): Treat time series as natural language processing
Hypergraph Neural Networks (CityEVCP): Model higher-order relationships
Diffusion Networks (STEV-DiffNet): Adaptive graph diffusion for long-range dependencies

how long data is needed for 1-5 hours of -prediction and can I use overlap window for training?



For **hourly** forecasting of **session-start counts** at each charging station (CS), there are two different “how long” questions that matter:

1. **How much past history per training example** (lookback window (L)) do you feed the model to predict the next (H=1\ldots5) hours?
2. **How many weeks/months/years of data** do you need overall to train a stable model and generalize?

I’ll answer both, then address **overlapping windows** (yes, you should use them—carefully).

---

## 1) How much history (L) do you need to predict 1–5 hours ahead?

Your target is:

[
y_{i,t} = #{\text{sessions that start at station } i \text{ during hour } t}.
]

For horizons (H \in [1,5]) hours, the most useful signals usually come from:

* **recent hours** (short-term momentum and local effects),
* **daily seasonality** (hour-of-day),
* **weekly seasonality** (day-of-week).

That implies (L) should cover at least a full day, and often more.

### Recommended lookback lengths (hourly)

* **Minimum workable**: (L = 24) hours
  Captures the daily pattern; can be enough for (H=1) at many sites.
* **Strong default**: (L = 48) to (72) hours
  Helps stabilize under day-to-day noise; usually improves 1–5 hour horizons.
* **If behavior is strongly weekly**: (L = 168) hours (1 week)
  Especially if weekday/weekend differences are big.

### A high-performing trick (often beats simply increasing L)

Even with moderate (L), add explicit seasonal lags as features:

* (y_{i,t-24}) (same hour yesterday)
* (y_{i,t-168}) (same hour last week)

This often gives you “weekly awareness” without needing a huge receptive field.

---

## 2) How much total data do you need overall?

This depends on whether you train:

* a **global model** shared across all stations (typical for ST-GNN), or
* separate per-station models (not recommended here).

You’re doing a **global ST-GNN**, so each station contributes windows, and the model pools patterns across stations. That means you need enough data to learn:

* temporal seasonality (daily/weekly),
* cross-station heterogeneity,
* graph correlations.

### Rule-of-thumb for hourly session-start forecasting

* **Bare minimum** (to get something training without collapsing):
  ~ **4–6 weeks** of data *across the network* (not necessarily per station).
  This covers multiple weekdays/weekends.
* **Reasonable** for stable performance:
  **3–6 months** (captures more variability: weather regimes, school vs non-school, etc.).
* **Best** if you care about long-term robustness and seasonal shifts:
  **≥ 12 months** (annual seasonality + enough rare events).

### What about stations that only exist late (e.g., open in 2025)?

You do **not** need the same length for every station.

* A station with **1 year of history** is absolutely enough for 1–5 hour forecasting.
* A station with **a few weeks** can still be used—your model will rely more on:

  * station static features (location, ports, power),
  * neighboring stations via the graph,
  * global seasonality patterns.

A practical policy many teams use:

* include a station in training loss only after it has at least (L + H) hours of history, and optionally after it has at least **2–4 weeks** of presence (to avoid pure cold-start noise).

---

## 3) Can you use overlapping windows for training?

Yes — **overlapping sliding windows are standard** and usually the best way to train deep time-series models, including ST-GNNs.

### The standard supervised windowing

For each station (i), at each time (t):

* Input: (\mathbf{x}_{i,t-L+1:t})
* Output: (\mathbf{y}_{i,t+1:t+H})

If you slide (t) forward by 1 hour, windows overlap heavily.

### Why overlap is good

* You get many training samples.
* You use data efficiently.
* Mini-batches mix many local contexts → optimization is smoother.

### The real risk: leakage and “fake generalization”

Overlapping windows are only a problem if you split train/val/test incorrectly.

**Correct approach**:

1. Split by time first (e.g., train: 2018–2024, val: early 2025, test: later 2025).
2. Generate windows **within** each split only.

**Incorrect approach**:

* Generate all windows first, then randomly split windows → massive leakage (because adjacent windows share most timestamps).

### Use a “gap” near boundaries (recommended)

Because of autocorrelation, add a gap of at least (L) hours between splits:

* Train ends at time (T_{\text{train}})
* Validation begins at (T_{\text{train}} + L)

This prevents windows in val from using almost the same history as the last train windows.

---

## 4) Should you always use stride = 1 hour?

Stride (s) = how much you shift the window each training sample.

* **Stride = 1** hour: maximum samples, more correlation between samples.
* **Stride = 2–6** hours: fewer, less redundant samples, faster training.

### Practical recommendation

* Start with **stride = 1** (best accuracy baseline).
* If training is slow or you see overfitting, try **stride = 2 or 3**.
* Another good compromise: keep stride=1 but **randomly subsample windows** each epoch.

---

## 5) Extra caution for ST-GNN specifically

Two subtle leakage channels people miss:

### A) Graph built using full-history demand similarity

If you build edges using correlation/DTW computed on **2018–2025 including test**, you leak future information.

Fix:

* compute similarity edges **only on training period**, or
* prefer static edges (distance), or
* learn adaptive adjacency end-to-end (less leakage risk if trained only on train).

### B) Normalization leakage

If you standardize using global mean/std over all years, that leaks.

Fix:

* compute scalers on **training only**, apply to val/test.

---

If you want a strong, defensible baseline:

* Resolution: **hourly**
* Target: session-start count (y_{i,t})
* Horizon: **H = 5** (predict next 1–5 hours jointly, direct multi-horizon)
* Lookback: **L = 72** (3 days)

  * add lag features (t-24), (t-168)
* Window stride: **1** hour (or 2 if heavy)
* Split: time-based, with a **gap = L** at boundaries
* Loss: masked **Negative Binomial** (best for counts) or masked MAE as baseline

Got it: **hourly resolution**, and your target is:

[
y_{i,t} ;=; #{\text{sessions that START at station } i \text{ during hour } t}.
]

That’s a clean “arrival-count” definition (and it avoids the long-duration complication you’d get if you tried to forecast “active sessions” or “occupied ports”). With this definition, **Level 2 vs DCFC mostly affects the *distribution of arrivals***, not the label mechanics.

## 1) What “short‑term prediction” means in your setup

In forecasting, “short-term” is not a single universal number; it’s defined relative to:

* the **decision cadence** (what action you want to take),
* the **signal dynamics** (how quickly demand changes),
* the **availability of covariates** (weather forecasts, events, etc.).

For **hourly station-level session arrivals**, the most standard operational horizons are:

### Very short-term / nowcasting

* **1-step ahead**: predict the **next hour** ((h=1))
  [
  \hat y_{i,t+1}
  ]
* Purpose: near-real-time staffing, charger availability alerts, immediate rebalancing decisions, short-term grid constraints.

### Short-term (in many EVCS papers and operations contexts)

* **Multi-hour ahead**: predict **next 1–5 hours** ((h \in {1,\dots,5}))
  [
  [\hat y_{i,t+1},\dots,\hat y_{i,t+5}]
  ]
* Purpose: near-term congestion risk, shift scheduling, demand response windows, station maintenance dispatch planning.

### Day-ahead

* **24-hour ahead** (or “tomorrow hourly profile”):
  [
  [\hat y_{i,t+1},\dots,\hat y_{i,t+24}]
  ]
* Purpose: day-ahead energy procurement (if that matters), operations planning for tomorrow, expected congestion periods across stations, scheduling maintenance windows.

So in your context:

* “short-term” most naturally means **1–5 hours ahead**.
* “day-ahead” is **24 hours ahead** (often as a full profile).

---

## 2) What changes when you move from 1-hour ahead → multi-hour → day-ahead?

This is the key ML answer: **the problem’s conditional structure changes**, and so should your modeling choices.

### A) Predicting 1 hour ahead ((h=1)): “local dynamics”

Most of your predictive power comes from:

* recent history (last few hours),
* time-of-day,
* day-of-week,
* near-station spatial coupling (neighbor stations).

A spatiotemporal GNN can do very well here with a moderate history window.

**Typical input window** (hourly):

* (L = 24) to 72 hours (1–3 days), sometimes plus weekly lags.

### B) Predicting 1–5 hours ahead: “multi-step uncertainty + drift”

Now you’re forecasting beyond immediate inertia. Two major effects appear:

1. **Error propagation** becomes an issue if you forecast iteratively.
2. You start needing stronger representation of daily periodicity and spatial propagation.

For (H=5) horizons, a good model should output a 5-dimensional horizon vector per node:
[
\hat{\mathbf y}*{i,t} = (\hat y*{i,t+1},\dots,\hat y_{i,t+5})
]

**Typical input window**:

* (L = 48) to 168 hours (2 days to 1 week), depending on how weekly patterns matter.

### C) Day-ahead ((H=24)): “seasonality dominates”

Day-ahead is much more about:

* **calendar structure** (weekday/weekend),
* **repeating daily profiles**,
* **weekly seasonality**,
* and exogenous forecastable covariates (weather forecasts, events).

Also, for day-ahead you should assume you do **not** know future short-term shocks (accidents, sudden spikes), so the model is learning the *expected* profile.

**Typical input window**:

* (L = 168) hours (1 week) is a common minimum;
* sometimes 2–4 weeks depending on stability.

---

## 3) Multi-step forecasting: the biggest modeling fork

When you say “predict day-ahead” or “predict next 5 hours”, you must choose **how** to do multi-step prediction. There are three canonical strategies:

### Strategy 1: Iterative (recursive) forecasting

Train 1-step model:
[
\hat y_{t+1} = f(y_{t-L+1:t}, X_{t-L+1:t})
]
Then roll forward:

* feed (\hat y_{t+1}) back in to predict (\hat y_{t+2}), etc.

**Pros**

* simplest training
* one model for all horizons

**Cons**

* error accumulation (“drift”)
* often weak for day-ahead

This is usually **not the best** if you care about 24-hour profiles.

### Strategy 2: Direct multi-horizon (multi-output) forecasting

Single model outputs all horizons at once:
[
(\hat y_{t+1}, \dots, \hat y_{t+H}) = f(\text{history})
]

**Pros**

* avoids error accumulation
* best general choice for H=5 or H=24

**Cons**

* slightly heavier model
* must handle horizon-specific difficulty

This is the approach I’d recommend for you if you want 1–5 hours or day-ahead.

### Strategy 3: Direct per-horizon models

Train separate models for each horizon (h):
[
\hat y_{t+h} = f_h(\text{history})
]

**Pros**

* can maximize accuracy per horizon

**Cons**

* heavy to maintain
* less elegant, more risk of inconsistency across horizons

---

## 4) What “demand” means for your target and why hourly helps

You said: “# of sessions at each CS”.

Make the definition explicit and consistent:

### Recommended label definition (hourly)

For each station (i) and hour bucket (t):

* (y_{i,t}) = count of sessions whose **start timestamp** falls in hour (t).

Why “start” is best:

* It’s a pure arrival process (like a point process aggregated into bins).
* It is less sensitive to long charging durations (L2 vs DCFC).
* It aligns well with operational interest (“how many arrivals next hour?”).

Alternative labels that you are *not* choosing (but good to be aware of):

* **Active sessions** (how many sessions overlap the hour) → dominated by duration.
* **Occupancy** (#ports busy) → needs port inventory per station and duration.
* **Energy per hour** → needs allocation over time, sensitive to duration and power curves.

So your choice is good and makes the modeling cleaner.

---

## 5) Model implications: your target is a *count process*

Hourly session counts are:

* nonnegative integers,
* often zero-inflated at low-utilization stations,
* overdispersed (variance > mean) at many stations.

This matters because many ST-GNN papers default to MSE/MAE, but for counts you often do better with a **count likelihood**:

### If you want the statistically principled approach

Use a Negative Binomial (NB) or Poisson head:

* Model outputs parameters (e.g., NB mean (\mu_{i,t}) and dispersion (r_i)),
* Train with log-likelihood:
  [
  \mathcal{L} = -\sum_{t,i} M_{t,i}\log p(y_{i,t}\mid \mu_{i,t}, r_i)
  ]

**Why NB**: real-world arrivals are usually overdispersed relative to Poisson.

### If you want simplest baseline

MAE loss on counts works surprisingly well, but it won’t capture uncertainty and can underfit low-count regimes.

If later you care about probabilistic forecasts (“what’s the chance arrivals exceed 10?”), you’ll want NB/Poisson or quantiles.

---

## 6) So what horizon should you pick?

Tie it to your use-case:

* If you care about **immediate congestion / staffing** → start with **1-hour ahead** and **1–5 hours ahead**.
* If you care about “tomorrow’s profile” planning → do **day-ahead (24h)**.
* If you want a clean academic structure: report multiple horizons:

  * (H=1) (1 hour),
  * (H=3) or (H=5),
  * (H=24).

This is common in spatiotemporal forecasting papers: show performance degradation as horizon increases.

---

## 7) What should change in your GNN when horizon changes?

### For 1-hour ahead

* moderate receptive field is enough
* graph helps capture short-term spatial substitution (nearby stations)

### For 1–5 hours

* multi-horizon output head
* longer temporal receptive field (at least 2–7 days)
* graph + temporal becomes more important

### For day-ahead (24h)

* **strong seasonal encoding** (hour-of-day, day-of-week)
* bigger receptive field (≥ 1 week)
* direct multi-horizon is strongly preferred
* consider modeling per-station base profiles + residual GNN (a strong trick):

  * learn station-specific baseline profile (b_{i,hour,daytype}),
  * predict residual with GNN:
    [
    y_{i,t} = b_{i,\text{hour}(t),\text{dow}(t)} + r_{i,t}
    ]
    This often stabilizes day-ahead forecasting substantially.

You *can* do either, but it’s not a “DC Fast is always better” choice. The right decision depends on **what you want the target to mean** and whether you want one model to generalize across **two fundamentally different charging regimes**.

Below is the clean way to reason about it and what I’d recommend in practice for your exact setting (multi‑provider, mostly DC fast, ChargePoint has both).

---

## 1) DC Fast vs Level 2 are different *generative processes*

Even if you aggregate everything to “sessions per hour” or “kWh per hour”, DCFC and L2 differ in:

* **dwell time / service time distribution** (L2 is long-tailed; DCFC is short),
* **user intent** (en-route vs destination),
* **diurnal patterns** (workplace L2 often has different peaks than highway DCFC),
* **capacity coupling** (L2 occupancy dynamics dominate availability; DCFC is more arrival‑rate dominated),
* **kWh/time mapping** (L2 energy is spread over many bins; DCFC energy is concentrated).

So mixing them inside a single node target often creates **multi-modality** and **heteroscedasticity** that a plain ST‑GNN may fit poorly unless you model type explicitly.

---

## 2) The key: what exactly is your “demand” target?

### A) If your target is **# of sessions (arrivals) per interval**

If you define demand as “number of sessions that *start* in [t, t+Δ)”, then **session duration doesn’t directly affect the label**.

* In that case, you *can* include both DCFC and L2.
* But you still risk **negative transfer** because the spatial correlations and temporal seasonality differ by charger type.

Best practice:

* Keep both types **but** make port type explicit (or separate heads / separate models).

### B) If your target is **kWh per interval** (load forecasting)

Then session duration matters a lot, because you must decide how to allocate energy in time.

If you simply assign all kWh to the start time bin, L2 becomes badly mis-modeled (most of its energy is delivered later). For kWh forecasting, the most defensible approach is:

* allocate each session’s kWh across the bins it spans (uniformly over charging time, or using a charging-rate profile if you have power traces),
* then aggregate per station per bin.

In this setting, mixing L2 and DCFC without modeling type/power rating is much more likely to degrade performance.

### C) If your target is **occupancy / #ports busy**

Then L2 is *very important* (long sessions dominate occupancy), and DCFC is a different occupancy regime. You almost certainly want separate modeling or type-aware modeling.

---

## 3) A very practical point: what is your “node”?

This is often the deciding factor.

### Option 1 — Node = **station**

If a station has both L2 and DCFC ports, the station-level time series is a **mixture**. You can still do it, but the model must learn mixed dynamics.

### Option 2 — Node = **EVSE / connector (port)**

Given your schema, you often have `EVSE ID`, `Port Number`, `Plug Type`, `Port Type`, etc.

If you set the node to EVSE/port:

* port type is fixed per node,
* duration regime is consistent,
* your graph can include:

  * **intra-station edges** between ports at the same station,
  * **inter-station edges** by distance / similarity.

This is, from an ML perspective, a *cleaner* formulation for mixed infrastructure.

If you’re undecided: **for DCFC vs L2, defining nodes as EVSEs is usually the best engineering move**.

---

## 4) So should you filter ChargePoint to only “DC Fast”?

### When filtering to DC Fast is the best choice

Filter to DC Fast (and drop L2) if:

* Your other providers are all DCFC and you want a **single consistent system**.
* Your operational goal is **short-term DCFC planning** (queue risk, demand response, peak power management).
* You want the simplest first model and cleanest benchmarking.

This is also the best option if you’re predicting **kWh per short bin** (e.g., 15–60 minutes) and you don’t want to implement careful energy allocation across long L2 sessions yet.

### When keeping Level 2 is better

Keep L2 if:

* You want a model that covers **all public charging behavior**, not just DCFC.
* You care about **occupancy/availability**, where L2 dominates dynamics.
* You have enough metadata (charger power, #ports, site type) to let the model condition on charger class.

But: I would *not* keep L2 “as-is” without making the model type-aware. Otherwise you’ll often see:

* worse calibration,
* poor generalization across stations,
* the graph message passing can smear patterns across incompatible node types.

## 5) Best practice recommendation for your case

Because you said:

* most tabs are **all DC Fast**,
* price is basically constant (so pricing effects are minimal),
* goal is **short-term #sessions or kWh**,

I’d recommend this workflow:

### Step 1 — Build a strong DCFC baseline (fast path)

* Use **only DC Fast** across all providers (including ChargePoint DC Fast subset).
* Node = **EVSE** if possible; otherwise station.
* Target:

  * sessions-start count per Δ (very clean), and/or
  * kWh per Δ (but computed properly).
* Model: an adaptive ST-GNN (Graph WaveNet-style or ASTGRN-style), with masking for stations that appear later.

This gives you a high-quality baseline aligned with most of your data.

### Step 2 — Add L2 as a *separate regime* (don’t mix blindly)

Then either:

**(A) Two-model approach (simple & strong):**

* Train one model for DCFC, one model for L2.
* Optionally share embeddings or pretrain on DCFC then finetune for L2 (transfer).

**(B) One model, two heads (mixture-of-experts flavor):**

* Shared spatiotemporal encoder,
* separate output heads conditioned on `port_type`,
* optionally gating network chooses head weights.

**(C) Heterogeneous GNN (most principled):**

* node types: {DCFC, L2},
* relation types / edge types,
* type-specific parameters.

If you want “best performance + clean science,” (A) or (B) is often the sweet spot.

* For **DCFC**, short bins (15–60 min) make sense because events are short.

If your target is session starts:

If your target is kWh:
