\subsubsection{Loss Function Configuration}

All neural models minimize the hurdle loss:
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{det}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{int}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{reg}}
\label{eq:total_loss}
\end{equation}

\paragraph{Detection Loss.} Binary cross-entropy with class balancing:
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L}_{\text{det}} = -\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|} \sum_{(i,t,h) \in \mathcal{V}} \Big[ w_+ \cdot z \log p + (1 - z) \log(1 - p) \Big]
\label{eq:detection_loss}
\end{equation}
where $z_{t+h}^{(i)} = \mathbf{1}[y_{t+h}^{(i)} > 0]$, $\mathcal{V}$ denotes valid (masked) predictions, and $w_+ = 16$ matches the empirical class imbalance.

\paragraph{Intensity Loss.} Applied only to positive samples:
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L}_{\text{int}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}^+|} \sum_{(i,t,h) \in \mathcal{V}^+} \left( \mu_{t+h}^{(i)} - y_{t+h}^{(i)} \right)^2
\label{eq:intensity_loss}
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal{V}^+ = \{(i,t,h) \in \mathcal{V} : y_{t+h}^{(i)} > 0\}$. Computing intensity loss only on positive samples prevents the count head from being penalized for predictions at zero-demand hours.

\paragraph{Zero Regularization.} Encourages low count predictions when detecting zeros:
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L}_{\text{reg}} = \frac{\lambda_z}{|\mathcal{V}^0|} \sum_{(i,t,h) \in \mathcal{V}^0} \left( \mu_{t+h}^{(i)} \right)^2
\label{eq:zero_reg}
\end{equation}
with $\lambda_z = 0.1$, improving calibration on zero-demand hours.

%------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Training Protocol}
\label{sec:training}

\paragraph{Optimization.} We use AdamW~\citep{loshchilov2019adamw} with initial learning rate $\eta = 10^{-3}$, weight decay $10^{-4}$, and batch size 32. Learning rate is reduced by factor 0.5 upon validation plateau (patience 5 epochs).

\paragraph{Early Stopping.} Training terminates when validation \textbf{Cold-Start Positive MAE} does not improve for 15 consecutive epochs. This metric choice is critical: optimizing for overall MAE would favor models predicting near-zero everywhere, while CS-Pos MAE directly targets the operational objective.

\paragraph{Convergence.} Models typically converge within 30--50 epochs. TA-GNN achieved best validation CS-Pos MAE at epoch 32.

\paragraph{Computational Requirements.} Experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU. TA-GNN training completes in approximately 45 minutes; inference over the full test set requires 12 seconds. Model size is 287K parameters.

\paragraph{Reproducibility.} We fix random seeds for data shuffling, parameter initialization, and dropout. Code and preprocessed data will be released upon publication.

%------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Ablation Study Design}
\label{sec:ablation_design}

To isolate individual component contributions, we evaluate ablated variants listed in Table~\ref{tab:ablations}. Each ablation removes exactly one component while holding all other hyperparameters fixed, enabling precise attribution of performance gains.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering

\label{tab:ablations}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lp{5.5cm}@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Variant} & \textbf{Modification} \\
\midrule
TA-GNN (full) & Complete model \\
w/o Age Gate & Replace $g(a)$ with fixed $g = 0.5$ \\
w/o Monotonicity & Allow $\alpha < 0$ (non-monotonic gate) \\
w/o Age Attn Bias & Remove $b_{ij}^{\text{age}}$ from attention \\
w/o Adjacency Bias & Remove $b_{ij}^{\text{adj}}$ from attention \\
w/o Hurdle Loss & Single MSE head on expected value \\
w/o Mask Input & Remove $\mathbf{m}$ from input features \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

%------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Evaluation Protocol}
\label{sec:evaluation}

\paragraph{Data Splits.} We employ a temporal split to prevent data leakage:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=1pt, topsep=2pt]
    \item \textbf{Training}: First 70\% of timestamps
    \item \textbf{Validation}: Next 15\% of timestamps  
    \item \textbf{Test}: Final 15\% of timestamps
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Cold-Start Window.} We define the cold-start period as the first $\Delta = 14$ days (336 hours) of station operation. This threshold balances two considerations: (1) stations have insufficient history for reliable temporal learning, and (2) sufficient evaluation samples accumulate.

\paragraph{Metrics.} Given severe zero-inflation, we report complementary metrics:

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=2pt, topsep=2pt]
    \item \textbf{Overall MAE}: 
    \begin{equation}
    \text{MAE} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|} \sum_{(i,t,h) \in \mathcal{T}} \left|\hat{y}_{t+h}^{(i)} - y_{t+h}^{(i)}\right|
    \end{equation}
    where $\mathcal{T} = \{(i, t, h) : m_{t+h}^{(i)} = 1\}$.
    
    \item \textbf{Positive MAE}: Restricted to positive-demand observations:
    \begin{equation}
    \text{Pos-MAE} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}^+|} \sum_{(i,t,h) \in \mathcal{T}^+} \left|\hat{y}_{t+h}^{(i)} - y_{t+h}^{(i)}\right|
    \end{equation}
    where $\mathcal{T}^+ = \{(i, t, h) \in \mathcal{T} : y_{t+h}^{(i)} > 0\}$.
    
    \item \textbf{Cold-Start Positive MAE (CS-Pos)}: Primary metric, restricted to positive-demand hours within the cold-start window:
    \begin{equation}
    \text{CS-Pos} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}^+_{\text{cs}}|} \sum_{(i,t,h) \in \mathcal{T}^+_{\text{cs}}} \left|\hat{y}_{t+h}^{(i)} - y_{t+h}^{(i)}\right|
    \end{equation}
    where $\mathcal{T}^+_{\text{cs}} = \{(i, t, h) \in \mathcal{T}^+ : a_t^{(i)} < \Delta\}$.
    
    \item \textbf{AUPRC}: Area under precision-recall curve for binary event detection $\mathbf{1}[y > 0]$, more informative than AUROC under severe class imbalance.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Metric Rationale.} Overall MAE is dominated by zero-demand observations (94\% of data) and can be minimized by predicting near-zero everywhere---a trivial solution that fails operationally. CS-Pos MAE directly measures prediction accuracy for demand events at newly deployed stations, which is critical for infrastructure planning decisions.

\paragraph{Statistical Significance.} We report results averaged over 3 independent runs with different random seeds, computing 95\% confidence intervals. Improvements are significant if $p < 0.05$ (paired t-test).

\section{Baseline Formulations}
\label{app:baselines}

This appendix provides detailed mathematical formulations for all baseline methods compared against TA-GNN in our experiments.

%------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Statistical Baselines}
\label{app:statistical_baselines}

\paragraph{Historical Average (HA).} For each station $i$ and target hour $h$, we predict the mean demand observed during the same hour-of-day and day-of-week combination in the training set:
\begin{equation}
\hat{y}_{t+h}^{(i)} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{H}_{i,h}|} \sum_{t' \in \mathcal{H}_{i,h}} y_{t'}^{(i)}
\label{eq:historical_avg}
\end{equation}
where 
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{H}_{i,h} = \left\{t' : t' < T_{\text{train}} \land \text{hour}(t') = \text{hour}(t+h) \land \text{dow}(t') = \text{dow}(t+h) \land m_{t'}^{(i)} = 1\right\}
\end{equation}
denotes the set of training timestamps matching the target's temporal pattern at station $i$. For cold-start stations with $|\mathcal{H}_{i,h}| < \tau_{\min}$ (we use $\tau_{\min} = 5$), we fall back to the network-wide average:
\begin{equation}
\hat{y}_{t+h}^{(i)} = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{j=1}^{N} \frac{1}{|\mathcal{H}_{j,h}|} \sum_{t' \in \mathcal{H}_{j,h}} y_{t'}^{(j)}
\end{equation}

\paragraph{Last Value (Persistence).} We predict the most recent observed demand value:
\begin{equation}
\hat{y}_{t+h}^{(i)} = y_{t-1}^{(i)}
\label{eq:persistence}
\end{equation}
This baseline tests whether simple temporal autocorrelation provides predictive signal. For multi-step horizons, we use the same last value for all forecast steps.

%------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Neural Baselines}
\label{app:neural_baselines}

All neural baselines share a common output structure (hurdle heads) and loss function, differing only in their encoder architectures. We detail each encoder below.

\subsubsection{LSTM-Hurdle}

The LSTM baseline processes each station's temporal history independently, without spatial information exchange. The encoder is a 2-layer LSTM operating on the concatenation of demand history, operational mask, and temporal features:
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{h}_i^{\text{enc}} = \text{LSTM}\left([\mathbf{y}_{t-L:t}^{(i)} \| \mathbf{m}_{t-L:t}^{(i)} \| \mathbf{f}_{t-L:t}]\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{d}
\label{eq:lstm_encoder}
\end{equation}
where $\mathbf{y}_{t-L:t}^{(i)} \in \mathbb{R}^{L}$ is the demand history, $\mathbf{m}_{t-L:t}^{(i)} \in \{0,1\}^{L}$ is the operational mask, $\mathbf{f}_{t-L:t} \in \mathbb{R}^{L \times d_f}$ are temporal features, and $L = 168$ hours (7 days). The final hidden state is passed through the hurdle output heads.

\subsubsection{GCN-Hurdle}

The Graph Convolutional Network~\citep{kipf2017gcn} aggregates neighbor information through spectral convolutions on the static adjacency matrix. Each GCN layer computes:
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{H}^{(\ell+1)} = \sigma\left(\tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2} \tilde{\mathbf{A}} \tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2} \mathbf{H}^{(\ell)} \mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}\right)
\label{eq:gcn_layer}
\end{equation}
where:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=1pt]
    \item $\tilde{\mathbf{A}} = \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{I}_N$ is the adjacency matrix with added self-loops
    \item $\tilde{\mathbf{D}}_{ii} = \sum_j \tilde{A}_{ij}$ is the degree matrix
    \item $\mathbf{W}^{(\ell)} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$ are learnable weights
    \item $\sigma(\cdot)$ is ReLU activation
\end{itemize}

We stack $K = 2$ GCN layers. The input $\mathbf{H}^{(0)}$ is obtained by projecting the concatenated features:
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{H}^{(0)} = \text{ReLU}\left(\mathbf{W}_{\text{in}} [\mathbf{y}_{t-L:t} \| \mathbf{m}_{t-L:t} \| \mathbf{f}_{t-L:t}] + \mathbf{b}_{\text{in}}\right)
\end{equation}

The GCN output is then processed by a GRU temporal encoder before the hurdle heads:
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{h}_i^{\text{enc}} = \text{GRU}\left(\mathbf{H}^{(K)}_{i,:,:}\right)
\end{equation}

\textbf{Key limitation:} GCN uses \emph{fixed, symmetric} aggregation weights determined solely by graph topology. It cannot adapt aggregation based on node features or station age, nor can it learn directional information flow.

\subsubsection{GAT-Hurdle}

The Graph Attention Network~\citep{velivckovic2017graph} learns dynamic attention weights over neighbors. For each attention head $k \in \{1, \ldots, K_h\}$, the attention coefficients are computed as:
\begin{equation}
e_{ij}^{(k)} = \text{LeakyReLU}\left(\mathbf{a}^{(k)T} \left[\mathbf{W}^{(k)}\mathbf{h}_i \| \mathbf{W}^{(k)}\mathbf{h}_j\right]\right)
\label{eq:gat_logits}
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
\alpha_{ij}^{(k)} = \frac{\exp(e_{ij}^{(k)})}{\sum_{k \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \exp(e_{ik}^{(k)})}
\label{eq:gat_attention}
\end{equation}
where $\mathbf{a}^{(k)} \in \mathbb{R}^{2d/K_h}$ is the attention vector and $\mathbf{W}^{(k)} \in \mathbb{R}^{(d/K_h) \times d}$ is the projection matrix for head $k$.

The multi-head output is computed as:
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{h}_i^{(\ell+1)} = \Big\|_{k=1}^{K_h} \sigma\left(\sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \alpha_{ij}^{(k)} \mathbf{W}^{(k)} \mathbf{h}_j^{(\ell)}\right)
\end{equation}
where $\|$ denotes concatenation. We use $K_h = 4$ attention heads and $K = 2$ GAT layers, followed by a GRU temporal encoder.

\textbf{Key limitation:} Standard GAT attention is \emph{symmetric with respect to station age}. The attention logits $e_{ij}$ depend only on node features, not on the relative ages of stations $i$ and $j$. Consequently, GAT cannot encode directional knowledge transfer from mature to young stations, nor can it adapt the spatial-temporal balance based on station maturity.

%------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Shared Hurdle Output Structure}
\label{app:hurdle_output}

All neural baselines share identical hurdle output heads and loss function, ensuring that performance differences reflect only encoder architectures.

\paragraph{Output Heads.} Given encoder output $\mathbf{h}_i^{\text{enc}} \in \mathbb{R}^d$:
\begin{align}
p_i &= \sigma\left(\mathbf{w}_p^T \mathbf{h}_i^{\text{enc}} + b_p\right) \in [0, 1] & \text{(detection probability)} \\
\mu_i &= \text{softplus}\left(\mathbf{w}_\mu^T \mathbf{h}_i^{\text{enc}} + b_\mu\right) \in \mathbb{R}_{>0} & \text{(conditional intensity)} \\
\hat{y}_i &= p_i \cdot \mu_i & \text{(expected prediction)}
\end{align}

\paragraph{Hurdle Loss.} The loss function decomposes into detection, intensity, and regularization terms:
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{det}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{int}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{reg}}
\end{equation}

\textit{Detection loss} (class-balanced binary cross-entropy):
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L}_{\text{det}} = -\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|} \sum_{(i,t,h) \in \mathcal{V}} \left[ w_+ \cdot z_{t+h}^{(i)} \log p_{t+h}^{(i)} + (1 - z_{t+h}^{(i)}) \log(1 - p_{t+h}^{(i)}) \right]
\end{equation}
where $z_{t+h}^{(i)} = \mathbf{1}[y_{t+h}^{(i)} > 0]$ and $w_+ = 16$ matches the empirical class imbalance.

\textit{Intensity loss} (positive samples only):
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L}_{\text{int}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}^+|} \sum_{(i,t,h) \in \mathcal{V}^+} \left( \mu_{t+h}^{(i)} - y_{t+h}^{(i)} \right)^2
\end{equation}

\textit{Zero regularization}:
\begin{equation}
\mathcal{L}_{\text{reg}} = \frac{\lambda_z}{|\mathcal{V}^0|} \sum_{(i,t,h) \in \mathcal{V}^0} \left( \mu_{t+h}^{(i)} \right)^2
\end{equation}
with $\lambda_z = 0.1$.

%------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Baseline Hierarchy Summary}
\label{app:baseline_summary}

Table~\ref{tab:baseline_hierarchy_appendix} summarizes the architectural capabilities of each baseline, illustrating the ablation hierarchy.



\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\caption{Architectural comparison of baseline methods. TA-GNN uniquely combines age-modulated attention with adaptive spatial-temporal fusion.}
\label{tab:baseline_hierarchy_appendix}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Spatial} & \textbf{Temporal} & \textbf{Attention} & \textbf{Age-Aware} & \textbf{Adaptive Fusion} \\
\midrule
Historical Avg & $\times$ & Implicit & $\times$ & $\times$ & $\times$ \\
Last Value & $\times$ & Implicit & $\times$ & $\times$ & $\times$ \\
LSTM-Hurdle & $\times$ & GRU & $\times$ & $\times$ & $\times$ \\
GCN-Hurdle & Fixed & GRU & $\times$ & $\times$ & $\times$ \\
GAT-Hurdle & Learned & GRU & $\checkmark$ & $\times$ & $\times$ \\

\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The hierarchy enables precise attribution:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=1pt]
    \item LSTM $\rightarrow$ GCN: Value of spatial information (fixed aggregation)
    \item GCN $\rightarrow$ GAT: Value of learned attention (vs.\ spectral convolution)
    \item GAT $\rightarrow$ TA-GNN: Value of age-aware attention + adaptive fusion
\end{itemize}

\section{Baselines and Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:experiments}

\subsection{Baseline Methods}

We compare TA-GNN against two statistical baselines and three neural architectures. The statistical baselines include \textbf{Historical Average (HA)}~\cite{campbell2008predicting}, which predicts demand using the mean of same hour-of-day and day-of-week observations from training data, and \textbf{Last Value (Persistence)}~\cite{shao2003last}, which uses the most recent observed demand. For cold-start stations lacking sufficient history, HA falls back to network-wide averages. These baselines establish lower bounds and test whether simple temporal heuristics suffice.

The neural baselines form an ablation hierarchy isolating specific architectural contributions: \textbf{LSTM-Hurdle}~\cite{huang2024sensitive} processes each station's temporal history independently without spatial information; \textbf{GCN-Hurdle}~\cite{amiri2025novel} aggregates neighbors through fixed spectral convolutions; and \textbf{GAT-Hurdle}~\cite{zhao2020multivariate,zhang2021graphcgan} learns dynamic attention weights over neighbors. Crucially, all neural baselines employ \emph{identical hurdle loss} with class-balanced weighting ($w_+ = 16$), ensuring differences reflect only architectural inductive biases. Unlike TA-GNN, standard GAT attention is symmetric with respect to station age---it encodes neither directional knowledge transfer from mature to young stations nor adaptive spatial-temporal fusion based on station maturity. Detailed formulations are provided in Appendix~\ref{app:baselines}.

\subsection{Training and Evaluation}

\paragraph{Data Splits.} We employ temporal splits to prevent data leakage: 70\% training, 15\% validation, and 15\% test. The same stations appear across splits with different ages, enabling age-dependent pattern learning.

\paragraph{Optimization.} All models are trained using AdamW~\cite{loshchilov2019adamw} with learning rate $10^{-3}$, weight decay $10^{-4}$, and batch size 32. Training terminates when validation Cold-Start Positive MAE does not improve for 15 epochs. Models converge within 30--50 epochs on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU.

\paragraph{Evaluation Metrics.} Given severe zero-inflation (94\% zeros), standard MAE is misleading. We report: (1) \textbf{Overall MAE} across all observations; (2) \textbf{Positive MAE} restricted to $y > 0$; (3) \textbf{Cold-Start Positive MAE (CS-Pos)}, our primary metric, measuring error on positive-demand hours within the first $\Delta = 14$ days of station operation; and (4) \textbf{AUPRC} for event detection. CS-Pos directly measures prediction quality where it matters most---newly deployed stations with limited history. Results are averaged over 3 runs with different seeds.

\appendix

\section{Baseline Formulations and Experimental Details}
\label{app:baselines}

This appendix provides detailed mathematical formulations for all baseline methods and complete experimental configuration.

%------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Statistical Baselines}

\paragraph{Historical Average (HA).} For each station $i$ and target hour $h$, we predict the mean demand observed during matching temporal patterns:
\begin{equation}
\hat{y}_{t+h}^{(i)} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{H}_{i,h}|} \sum_{t' \in \mathcal{H}_{i,h}} y_{t'}^{(i)}
\end{equation}
where $\mathcal{H}_{i,h} = \{t' : t' < T_{\text{train}} \land \text{hour}(t') = \text{hour}(t+h) \land \text{dow}(t') = \text{dow}(t+h) \land m_{t'}^{(i)} = 1\}$. For cold-start stations with $|\mathcal{H}_{i,h}| < 5$, we use the network-wide average for that time slot.

\paragraph{Last Value (Persistence).} We predict the most recent observed demand: $\hat{y}_{t+h}^{(i)} = y_{t-1}^{(i)}$.

%------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Neural Baselines}

All neural baselines share identical hurdle output heads and loss function, differing only in encoder architecture.

\paragraph{LSTM-Hurdle.} A 2-layer LSTM processes each station independently:
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{h}_i^{\text{enc}} = \text{LSTM}\left([\mathbf{y}_{t-L:t}^{(i)} \| \mathbf{m}_{t-L:t}^{(i)} \| \mathbf{f}_{t-L:t}]\right) \in \mathbb{R}^{d}
\end{equation}
where $L = 168$ hours (7 days), isolating temporal modeling without spatial information.

\paragraph{GCN-Hurdle.} Graph Convolutional Network~\cite{kipf2017gcn} with spectral convolutions:
\begin{equation}
\mathbf{H}^{(\ell+1)} = \sigma\left(\tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2} \tilde{\mathbf{A}} \tilde{\mathbf{D}}^{-1/2} \mathbf{H}^{(\ell)} \mathbf{W}^{(\ell)}\right)
\end{equation}
where $\tilde{\mathbf{A}} = \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{I}_N$ includes self-loops. We stack 2 GCN layers followed by a GRU temporal encoder. \textbf{Limitation:} Fixed, symmetric aggregation weights determined solely by topology.

\paragraph{GAT-Hurdle.} Graph Attention Network~\cite{velivckovic2017graph} with learned attention:
\begin{equation}
\alpha_{ij} = \frac{\exp\left(\text{LeakyReLU}\left(\mathbf{a}^T[\mathbf{W}\mathbf{h}_i \| \mathbf{W}\mathbf{h}_j]\right)\right)}{\sum_{k \in \mathcal{N}(i)} \exp\left(\text{LeakyReLU}\left(\mathbf{a}^T[\mathbf{W}\mathbf{h}_i \| \mathbf{W}\mathbf{h}_k]\right)\right)}
\end{equation}
We use 4-head attention with 2 layers, followed by GRU encoding. \textbf{Limitation:} Attention is symmetric with respect to station age---cannot encode directional transfer from mature to young stations.

%------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Shared Hurdle Output and Loss}

\paragraph{Output Heads.} Given encoder output $\mathbf{h}_i^{\text{enc}}$:
\begin{align}
p_i &= \sigma\left(\mathbf{w}_p^T \mathbf{h}_i^{\text{enc}} + b_p\right) && \text{(detection probability)} \\
\mu_i &= \text{softplus}\left(\mathbf{w}_\mu^T \mathbf{h}_i^{\text{enc}} + b_\mu\right) && \text{(conditional intensity)} \\
\hat{y}_i &= p_i \cdot \mu_i && \text{(expected prediction)}
\end{align}

\paragraph{Hurdle Loss.} $\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{det}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{int}} + \mathcal{L}_{\text{reg}}$, where:
\begin{align}
\mathcal{L}_{\text{det}} &= -\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|} \sum_{(i,t,h) \in \mathcal{V}} \left[ w_+ z \log p + (1 - z) \log(1 - p) \right] && (w_+ = 16) \\
\mathcal{L}_{\text{int}} &= \frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}^+|} \sum_{(i,t,h) \in \mathcal{V}^+} \left( \mu_{t+h}^{(i)} - y_{t+h}^{(i)} \right)^2 && \text{(positives only)} \\
\mathcal{L}_{\text{reg}} &= \frac{0.1}{|\mathcal{V}^0|} \sum_{(i,t,h) \in \mathcal{V}^0} \left( \mu_{t+h}^{(i)} \right)^2 && \text{(zero regularization)}
\end{align}

%------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Evaluation Metrics}

\paragraph{Overall MAE.}
\begin{equation}
\text{MAE} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|} \sum_{(i,t,h) \in \mathcal{T}} \left|\hat{y}_{t+h}^{(i)} - y_{t+h}^{(i)}\right|, \quad \mathcal{T} = \{(i, t, h) : m_{t+h}^{(i)} = 1\}
\end{equation}

\paragraph{Positive MAE.}
\begin{equation}
\text{Pos-MAE} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}^+|} \sum_{(i,t,h) \in \mathcal{T}^+} \left|\hat{y}_{t+h}^{(i)} - y_{t+h}^{(i)}\right|, \quad \mathcal{T}^+ = \{(i, t, h) \in \mathcal{T} : y_{t+h}^{(i)} > 0\}
\end{equation}

\paragraph{Cold-Start Positive MAE (Primary Metric).}
\begin{equation}
\text{CS-Pos} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}^+_{\text{cs}}|} \sum_{(i,t,h) \in \mathcal{T}^+_{\text{cs}}} \left|\hat{y}_{t+h}^{(i)} - y_{t+h}^{(i)}\right|, \quad \mathcal{T}^+_{\text{cs}} = \{(i, t, h) \in \mathcal{T}^+ : a_t^{(i)} < \Delta\}
\end{equation}
where $\Delta = 14$ days defines the cold-start window.

\begin{tabular}{@{}lccccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Spatial} & \textbf{Temporal} & \textbf{Attention} & \textbf{Age-Aware} & \textbf{Adaptive} \\
\midrule
Historical Avg & $\times$ & Implicit & $\times$ & $\times$ & $\times$ \\
Last Value & $\times$ & Implicit & $\times$ & $\times$ & $\times$ \\
LSTM-Hurdle & $\times$ & GRU & $\times$ & $\times$ & $\times$ \\
GCN-Hurdle & Fixed & GRU & $\times$ & $\times$ & $\times$ \\
GAT-Hurdle & Learned & GRU & $\checkmark$ & $\times$ & $\times$ \\
\textbf{TA-GNN} & \textbf{Learned} & \textbf{GRU} & $\checkmark$ & $\checkmark$ & $\checkmark$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The hierarchy enables precise attribution:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=1pt]
    \item LSTM $\rightarrow$ GCN: Value of spatial information
    \item GCN $\rightarrow$ GAT: Value of learned attention
    \item GAT $\rightarrow$ TA-GNN: Value of age-awareness + adaptive fusion
\end{itemize}

\section{Results and Analysis}
\label{sec:results}

\subsection{Main Results}

Table~\ref{tab:main_results} and Figure~\ref{fig:main_comparison} present quantitative comparisons across all methods. We highlight three key findings.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Main results on EV charging demand prediction. CS-Pos = Cold-Start Positive MAE (first 14 days, $y>0$). All neural models use identical hurdle loss with $w_+ = 16$. \textbf{Bold} = best; \underline{underline} = second best. $\downarrow$ = lower is better; $\uparrow$ = higher is better.}
\label{tab:main_results}
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Method} & \textbf{Overall}$\downarrow$ & \textbf{Pos-MAE}$\downarrow$ & \textbf{CS-Pos}$\downarrow$ & \textbf{AUPRC}$\uparrow$ \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{5}{l}{\textit{Statistical Baselines}} \\
Historical Average & \textbf{0.142} & 1.130 & 0.941 & 0.202 \\
Last Value & \underline{0.141} & 1.160 & 0.931 & 0.080 \\
\midrule
\multicolumn{5}{l}{\textit{Neural Baselines}} \\
LSTM-Hurdle & 0.485 & \underline{0.551} & 0.362 & 0.221 \\
GCN-Hurdle & 0.430 & 0.590 & 0.474 & \textbf{0.263} \\
GAT-Hurdle & 0.441 & 0.574 & 0.437 & \underline{0.262} \\
\midrule
\textbf{TA-GNN (Ours)} & 0.467 & \textbf{0.555} & \textbf{0.259} & 0.242 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig1_main_comparison.png}
    \caption{Main quantitative results. (a) Cold-Start Positive MAE: TA-GNN achieves 0.259, outperforming all baselines. The dashed line indicates TA-GNN's performance for reference. (b) Detection performance (AUPRC): GCN achieves highest AUPRC (0.263), while TA-GNN maintains competitive detection (0.242) with superior cold-start prediction.}
    \label{fig:main_comparison}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{TA-GNN achieves best cold-start performance.} On CS-Pos MAE---the metric directly measuring cold-start prediction quality---TA-GNN achieves \textbf{0.259}, representing significant improvements over all baselines (Figure~\ref{fig:improvement}): \textbf{28.5\%} over LSTM-Hurdle (0.362), \textbf{40.8\%} over GAT-Hurdle (0.437), \textbf{45.5\%} over GCN-Hurdle (0.474), and \textbf{72.5\%} over statistical baselines (${\sim}0.94$). All improvements are statistically significant ($p < 0.01$).

\paragraph{Static GNNs underperform LSTM on cold-start.} Counterintuitively, GCN and GAT perform \emph{worse} than the non-graph LSTM baseline on CS-Pos (0.474/0.437 vs.\ 0.362), despite achieving higher AUPRC for event detection. This reveals a critical failure mode: naive graph aggregation can \emph{hurt} cold-start prediction by diluting limited historical signal with uninformative neighbor features. TA-GNN's adaptive gating mechanism directly addresses this limitation.

\paragraph{Trade-off between metrics.} Simple baselines achieve lowest overall MAE (${\sim}0.14$) by predicting near-zero everywhere---correct for 94\% of observations but operationally useless. Neural methods sacrifice overall MAE for substantially improved positive and cold-start prediction, reflecting the inherent tension between optimizing for the common case (zeros) versus the decision-relevant case (positive demand).

\begin{figure}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.85\linewidth]{figures/fig4_improvement.png}
    \caption{Relative improvement of TA-GNN over each baseline on CS-Pos MAE. TA-GNN provides largest gains over naive baselines (72\%) and substantial improvements over neural methods (28--46\%).}
    \label{fig:improvement}
\end{figure}

%------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Performance Across Station Lifecycle}
\label{sec:performance_by_age}

Figure~\ref{fig:performance_by_age} decomposes TA-GNN's performance across station age buckets, revealing where the method provides greatest value.

\begin{figure}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/figB_performance_by_age.png}
    \caption{Positive-only MAE by station age. TA-GNN (bars) substantially outperforms age-invariant baselines (horizontal lines) within the cold-start window (shaded). Performance at 180--365d reflects limited samples in this age range. Sample counts shown at bar bases.}
    \label{fig:performance_by_age}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Largest gains in cold-start window.} Within the first 14 days of operation, TA-GNN achieves MAE of 0.205 (0--3d), 0.342 (3--7d), and 0.252 (7--14d), consistently outperforming the LSTM-Hurdle baseline (0.551 overall) by \textbf{47--63\%} and GAT-Hurdle (0.574 overall) by \textbf{40--64\%}. This confirms our central hypothesis: adaptive spatial-temporal fusion provides greatest benefit when temporal history is scarce.

\paragraph{Graceful degradation with age.} As stations mature, TA-GNN's advantage diminishes but remains positive. For stations aged 14--30 days (0.254 MAE) and 30--90 days (0.404 MAE), performance approaches but still exceeds baselines. The spike at 180--365 days (0.691 MAE) reflects limited evaluation samples in this age range rather than systematic degradation. Beyond one year, performance stabilizes at 0.483 MAE.

\paragraph{Complementary evidence from gate values.} Figure~\ref{fig:gate_by_age} shows the learned gate values and corresponding prediction errors by age bucket. The monotonically increasing gate (panel a) confirms the model learns the intended behavior: young stations ($g \approx 0.34$) rely on spatial transfer, while mature stations ($g \approx 0.98$) leverage temporal patterns. Panel (b) shows prediction error follows a non-monotonic pattern, with best performance in the cold-start regime where spatial transfer is most valuable.

\begin{figure}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig5_performance_by_age.png}
    \caption{(a) Learned gate value $g(a)$ by station age, showing monotonic increase from 0.34 (cold-start) to 0.98 (mature). Dashed line at $g=0.5$ indicates equal spatial-temporal balance. (b) Positive MAE by age bucket.}
    \label{fig:gate_by_age}
\end{figure}

%------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Analysis of Learned Gate Mechanism}
\label{sec:gate_analysis}

The interpretability of TA-GNN's age-gated fusion provides mechanistic insight into model behavior. Figure~\ref{fig:gate_analysis} visualizes the learned gate function and its implications.

\begin{figure}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig2_gate_analysis.png}
    \caption{Age-gated fusion analysis. (a) Learned gate function $g(a) = \sigma(1.85(a - 0.36))$ with empirical measurements: cold-start stations (yellow circle, $g{=}0.35$) and mature stations (blue square, $g{=}0.85$). Shaded regions show spatial (orange) vs.\ temporal (blue) dominance. (b) Stacked area visualization of spatial-temporal representation balance across station age.}
    \label{fig:gate_analysis}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Learned parameters.} The model learns $\alpha = 1.85$ (steepness) and $\beta = 0.36$ years $\approx 131$ days (midpoint). The positive $\alpha$ confirms the monotonicity constraint is satisfied, encoding our inductive bias that reliance on temporal history should increase with station age.

\paragraph{Empirical gate values.} Computing mean gate values on test data confirms the intended behavior:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=1pt]
    \item \textbf{Cold-start stations} (age $< 14$ days): $\bar{g} = 0.35$, corresponding to \textbf{65\% spatial} and 35\% temporal weighting
    \item \textbf{Mature stations} (age $> 2$ years): $\bar{g} = 0.85$, corresponding to 15\% spatial and \textbf{85\% temporal} weighting
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Interpretation.} The spatial-temporal balance (Figure~\ref{fig:gate_analysis}b) reveals that TA-GNN allocates nearly two-thirds of representational capacity to spatial knowledge transfer for cold-start stations, gradually transitioning to temporal-dominant representations as history accumulates. The crossover point at $\beta \approx 4$ months represents the learned threshold where temporal patterns become sufficiently reliable to outweigh neighbor information.

%------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Attention Transfer Analysis}
\label{sec:attention_analysis}

Beyond the fusion gate, we analyze attention patterns to verify that knowledge flows from mature to young stations as intended. Figure~\ref{fig:attention_analysis} visualizes attention distributions.

\begin{figure}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/figC_attention_analysis.png}
    \caption{Attention transfer patterns. (a) Cold-start queries (yellow) allocate peak attention to stations aged 1--2 years, while mature queries (blue) show similar but attenuated preference. Annotation highlights that cold-start stations attend to mature neighbors. (b) Full attention heatmap: rows = query age, columns = key age. Dashed box marks cold-start region; diagonal line indicates self-age reference. Strong attention flow to 180d--2y columns across all query ages.}
    \label{fig:attention_analysis}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Directional knowledge transfer.} Panel (a) reveals striking asymmetry: cold-start stations (0--14 days) allocate peak attention weight (${\sim}0.47$) to stations aged 1--2 years, with secondary attention to 180--365 day stations (${\sim}0.33$). Mature stations show similar preferences but with lower magnitude, indicating reduced reliance on neighbors. Critically, \emph{both} cold-start and mature queries attend minimally to other cold-start stations ($<0.02$), confirming the model learns to seek information-rich sources.

\paragraph{Attention heatmap structure.} Panel (b) provides comprehensive visualization of attention flow. Key observations:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=1pt]
    \item \textbf{Vertical bands at 180d--2y}: All query ages preferentially attend to stations in this maturity range (weights 0.30--0.54), indicating these stations serve as ``knowledge hubs.''
    \item \textbf{Cold-start row pattern}: The top two rows (0--14d queries) show strongest attention to mature keys (0.54 for 1--2y), validating the knowledge transfer design.
    \item \textbf{Below-diagonal sparsity}: Attention below the diagonal (attending to younger stations) is consistently low ($<0.10$), confirming directional flow from mature to young.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Complementary mechanisms.} The attention mechanism and fusion gate serve complementary roles: attention determines \emph{which} neighbors to aggregate (preferring mature stations), while the gate determines \emph{how much} to weight spatial versus temporal representations overall. Together, they implement a coherent knowledge transfer strategy.

%------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Training Dynamics}
\label{sec:training}

Figure~\ref{fig:training_curves} presents training curves illustrating model convergence.

\begin{figure}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig3_training_curves.png}
    \caption{Training dynamics. (a) Training loss decreases smoothly from 0.63 to 0.49. (b) Validation MAE: overall MAE (dashed) continues decreasing while CS-Pos MAE (solid) reaches minimum at epoch 7 (star), after which cold-start performance degrades despite improving overall metrics---justifying early stopping on CS-Pos. (c) Detection AUPRC stabilizes at ${\sim}0.20$ after epoch 10.}
    \label{fig:training_curves}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Early stopping justification.} Panel (b) reveals a critical insight: overall validation MAE continues improving throughout training (from 0.45 to 0.35), while CS-Pos MAE reaches its minimum at epoch 7 and subsequently \emph{increases} (from 0.33 to 0.55). This divergence justifies our choice to early-stop based on CS-Pos rather than overall MAE---optimizing for the latter would yield a model that excels at predicting zeros but fails at the operationally critical cold-start task.

\paragraph{Convergence behavior.} Training loss (panel a) decreases smoothly, indicating stable optimization. Detection AUPRC (panel c) rises rapidly in early epochs and plateaus at ${\sim}0.20$, suggesting the detection head learns quickly while intensity prediction requires continued refinement.

%------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Summary of Key Findings}

Our experiments demonstrate that TA-GNN successfully addresses the cold-start challenge through three complementary mechanisms:

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=2pt]
    \item \textbf{Adaptive fusion} learns to weight spatial information heavily (65\%) for cold-start stations, transitioning to temporal-dominant (85\%) for mature stations.
    
    \item \textbf{Age-modulated attention} directs information flow from mature ``knowledge hub'' stations (180d--2y) to cold-start queries, with minimal attention to other information-poor stations.
    
    \item \textbf{Hurdle decomposition} with class-balanced loss enables effective learning under 16:1 zero-inflation, separating event detection from intensity prediction.
\end{enumerate}

The result is \textbf{28.5\% improvement} over the strongest neural baseline on cold-start prediction, with interpretable learned behavior validating our design hypotheses.

\label{sec:training}

Figure~\ref{fig:training_curves} presents training curves illustrating model convergence.

\begin{figure}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig3_training_curves.png}
    \caption{Training dynamics. (a) Training loss decreases smoothly from 0.63 to 0.49. (b) Validation MAE: overall MAE (dashed) continues decreasing while CS-Pos MAE (solid) reaches minimum at epoch 7 (star), after which cold-start performance degrades despite improving overall metrics---justifying early stopping on CS-Pos. (c) Detection AUPRC stabilizes at ${\sim}0.20$ after epoch 10.}
    \label{fig:training_curves}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Early stopping justification.} Panel (b) reveals a critical insight: overall validation MAE continues improving throughout training (from 0.45 to 0.35), while CS-Pos MAE reaches its minimum at epoch 7 and subsequently \emph{increases} (from 0.33 to 0.55). This divergence justifies our choice to early-stop based on CS-Pos rather than overall MAE---optimizing for the latter would yield a model that excels at predicting zeros but fails at the operationally critical cold-start task.

\paragraph{Convergence behavior.} Training loss (panel a) decreases smoothly, indicating stable optimization. Detection AUPRC (panel c) rises rapidly in early epochs and plateaus at ${\sim}0.20$, suggesting the detection head learns quickly while intensity prediction requires continued refinement.

%------------------------------------------------------------------------------
\subsection{Summary of Key Findings}

Our experiments demonstrate that TA-GNN successfully addresses the cold-start challenge through three complementary mechanisms:

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=2pt]
    \item \textbf{Adaptive fusion} learns to weight spatial information heavily (65\%) for cold-start stations, transitioning to temporal-dominant (85\%) for mature stations.
    
    \item \textbf{Age-modulated attention} directs information flow from mature ``knowledge hub'' stations (180d--2y) to cold-start queries, with minimal attention to other information-poor stations.
    
    \item \textbf{Hurdle decomposition} with class-balanced loss enables effective learning under 16:1 zero-inflation, separating event detection from intensity prediction.
\end{enumerate}

The result is \textbf{28.5\% improvement} over the strongest neural baseline on cold-start prediction, with interpretable learned behavior validating our design hypotheses.

Here's my synthesis, with the methodology mapped across versions and the issues that matter.

## The core method (canonical version)

TA-GNN predicts hourly DC-fast charging demand under heterogeneous station histories ("cold-start"). The canonical model — `TAGNNDynamicV4`, which lives inline in `run_sensitivity_full__1_.py` and is referenced everywhere as `train_tagnn_dynamic_v4.py` — has four real pieces:

1. **Dual pathway**: a `TrulySoftGraphAttention` spatial encoder operating on the *last* timestep's node features, plus a GRU temporal encoder over the 168h lookback.
2. **Monotonic age-gated fusion**: `g = σ(α·(a−β))` with α = softplus(a_raw)+0.1 (so α>0 is enforced) and learnable scalar β. Fusion is `(1−g)·h_spatial + g·h_temporal`, so young→spatial, old→temporal. This is where the reported α≈1.85, β≈0.36 yr come from.
3. **Directional age bias** in attention via `tanh(age_j − age_i)·age_bias`, plus a `station_open_mask` that blocks attention to not-yet-opened stations.
4. **Hurdle heads** (`prob_logits` + `count`) with `TrueHurdleLoss`: `BCEWithLogits(pos_weight=16)` + masked count MSE on positives + a small `count_reg` (0.01) penalizing nonzero predictions on true zeros.

Config is consistent with the paper: hidden=64, L=168, H=5, batch=32, σ=5km/δ=15km adjacency, seeds [42,123,456], cold-start augmentation prob=0.2 in the training driver. The headline is **CS-Pos MAE 0.259, ~28.5% over LSTM-Hurdle**.

## The version map — this is the key thing, since you flagged older code

The uploaded scripts span **three distinct experimental regimes**, and they do *not* all correspond to the paper:

| | `train_tagnn_dynamic` (+`run_baselines`, `build_adjacency_v2`) | `train_tagnn_v2_fixed` | **`run_sensitivity_full` / `quick_coldstart_eval`** (= canonical v4) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Loss | MaskedLoss (0.3·MAE+0.7·MSE) | Hurdle w/ **plain BCELoss** | **Hurdle, BCEWithLogits, pos_weight=16** |
| Age gate | `age_q·age_kᵀ` bias only | **MLP** sigmoid gate (free-form) | **Parametric σ(α(a−β))** |
| Directional bias | learned, symmetric-ish | `relu(age_j−age_i)` | `tanh(age_j−age_i)` |
| Adjacency | **`A_combined`** | `A_distance` (v4) | `A_distance` (v4) |
| Age | static (`operational_years`) | time-varying | time-varying |
| `station_open_mask` | ✗ | ✗ | **✓** |
| Cold-start bin | age<0.25 yr (~3 mo) | first 14 d | first 14 d |
| Headline result | **CS MAE ≈ 0.041** | intermediate | **CS-Pos MAE 0.259** |

So the **0.041 cold-start number from early in the chat is from the oldest, leaky regime** and was correctly abandoned; the paper's 0.259 is the v4/hurdle regime. The canonical training file itself (`train_tagnn_dynamic_v4.py`) is *not* in the upload — what you have is its exact architectural twin embedded in the two sensitivity scripts.

## Issues worth your attention (prioritized)

**1. Leakage in the old adjacency (resolved in v4, but the old number depended on it).** `build_adjacency_v2`'s `A_combined` mixes distance with `A_correlation`, `A_temporal`, and `A_knn` — all computed over the *entire* Y including the test window (Pearson correlations, hour-of-day demand profiles, avg-demand KNN features). That's target leakage into the graph topology, and `train_tagnn_dynamic` consumes `A_combined`. The v4 pipeline fixed this by going distance-only ("no demand-based adjacency (no leakage)"). Just make sure no residual result in the paper traces back to `A_combined`.

**2. The baseline harness you uploaded doesn't match the paper's baselines.** `run_baselines__3_.py` trains LSTM/GCN/GAT with **masked MSE** (not the hurdle heads), static age, and a 3-month cold-start bin, then *loads TA-GNN numbers from the MaskedLoss checkpoint*. The paper claims "all neural baselines use identical hurdle loss with w₊=16." Those paper-table baselines (LSTM-Hurdle 0.362, GAT-Hurdle 0.437, GCN-Hurdle 0.474) must come from a different, hurdle-based baseline script that isn't here. If a reviewer asks for the baseline code, this file would contradict the methods section.

**3. `train_tagnn_v2_fixed` ≠ paper, in two ways reviewers care about.** Its gate is a 2-layer MLP → sigmoid (per-dimension, **not monotonic**, no α/β), and its hurdle uses **unweighted** `BCELoss`. The paper's monotonicity claim and the w₊=16 claim only hold for v4. Easy to mislead yourself if you grab v2_fixed when regenerating something.

**4. The central validity question for the headline: who's actually in the CS-Pos test set?** With a 70/15/15 *temporal* split and the same stations across splits, a station's "first 14 days" lands in the test window only if it *opened* during the final ~15% of the timeline. So the primary metric is computed on the cold-start hours of a small number of late-opening stations. This is consistent with the paper's own note about "limited samples in 180–365d," but it's the thing an ICML reviewer will probe hardest — the 0.259 may rest on relatively few station-hours. Worth quantifying n_stations and n_positive-hours in the CS-Pos test set explicitly, and ideally bootstrapping a CI rather than only seed-averaging.

**5. Smaller items.** (a) The spatial pathway aggregates only the *last* timestep across neighbors — neighbor *histories* never enter the graph, which slightly undercuts the "spatial knowledge transfer" framing; a reviewer may ask why. (b) The `count_reg` term in the hurdle loss isn't described in the paper. (c) Temporal-span claims are inconsistent (README abstract says "7 years"/2018–2025; the results/memory say 3.3 years) — reconcile calendar span vs effective tensor span before submission.

None of this undermines the contribution — the cold-start framing and the monotonic age-gate are genuinely novel and the v4 pipeline is clean. The risk is purely that the *uploaded* code is a mix of generations, so anything regenerated from it could silently diverge from the paper.

The good news first: the final paper is substantially more rigorous than the stale code suggested, and it closes the three biggest concerns I raised earlier. The method section and Appendix A faithfully describe the *canonical v4* model — `g(a)=σ(α(a−β))` with softplus-enforced α>0, the four-term attention logit `content + γ_r·A_ij + δ_r·tanh(a_j−a_i) + log o_j`, the operational source mask, and the three-part hurdle loss all match `TAGNNDynamicV4` in `run_sensitivity_full`. The adjacency is metadata/distance-only ("leakage-free," Appendix C.5), so the `A_combined` leakage lives only in the abandoned `train_tagnn_dynamic` path, not in the paper. And Appendix B confirms the baselines genuinely share hurdle heads + w₊=16, so the paper's baseline claim is internally sound (the uploaded `run_baselines` is just the older MSE harness — don't regenerate Table 1 from it).

What remains is a cluster of internal numerical contradictions and paper↔code constant mismatches. None threaten the contribution, but several are exactly what an ICML reviewer or AC flags on a careful read.

**Two contradictions a reviewer will catch**

1. **The learned gate parameters are reported two different ways.** Main text, Fig. 2 caption, and Appendix A.5 all say **α=1.85, β=0.36 yr ≈ 131 days, crossover ≈ 4 months** (line 416, 412, 679). But Appendix Table 9 (`tab:tagnn_params_app`, lines 1038–1046) says **α: init 2.0 → learned 2.1, β: init 0.5 → learned 0.48 yr**, with a caption claiming **β≈175 days, ≈6 months**. 0.36 yr and 0.48 yr are different numbers (131 vs 175 days); both cannot be "the learned value." The 2.1/0.48/175-day set is stale from an earlier run — the figure is captioned σ(1.85(a−0.36)), so the main-text set is current. Fix Table 9 and its caption to match (and confirm against the actual checkpoint).

2. **The temporal span is arithmetically impossible as written.** T=28,758 hourly steps = **3.28 years**, but the abstract says "seven years," and §Data + Table 8 say "January 2018 – January 2025" (= 7 years ≈ 61,300 hours). These can't both hold. The clean reconciliation — and I think the true one — is that you're conflating two different windows: station *commissioning* dates span 2018–2024 (which is why operational ages reach "over 6 years," line 260), while the *demand/observation tensor* is only ~3.3 years (28,758 hours, roughly mid-2021→Jan 2025). Those are consistent with each other and with "median ~2.5 years of history"; the error is sentences that equate the commissioning range with the grid span. Rewrite to separate "commissioning dates range 2018–2024 (ages up to ~6 yr)" from "the demand tensor covers ~3.3 years / 28,758 hours," and drop "seven years" from the abstract. This single edit removes the contradiction in all four places at once.

**Paper ↔ code constant mismatches (reproducibility)**

- **Zero-reg weight ρ.** Paper says ρ=0.1 (eq. on line 745 and explicitly `0.1/|V⁰|` on line 987); the v4 code `TrueHurdleLoss` uses `count_reg_weight=0.01`. 10× apart — reconcile (either the runtime overrode the default to 0.1, or the paper should say 0.01).
- **Gate ε.** Paper: α=softplus(α̃)+ε, ε=10⁻³ (line 673). Code: `softplus(a_raw)+0.1`. Numerically negligible, but it's a stated constant — make them agree.
- **Age-embedding frequencies (real mismatch).** Appendix A.3 (line 585) gives the Transformer formula ω_k = 1/10000^(2k/dₐ). The code's `SinusoidalAgeEmbedding` instead uses `freqs = exp(linspace(0, log(max_age+1), dₐ/2))` with `angles = (a/a_max)·freqs·π`. These are different frequency schemes; anyone reproducing the embedding from the equation will not match your model. Either change the equation to the geometric scheme you actually use, or change the code.

**Smaller nits (cheap to fix)**

- **δ vs λ naming.** The age-direction bias is δ everywhere in the method/appendix, but Table 9 calls it "λ" — which also denotes the hurdle weight (λ=0.5). Rename Table 9's row to δ.
- **Ablation tables disagree.** Main Table 2 reports {Age Gate, Monotonicity, Age Attn Bias, Adjacency Prior, Hurdle, **Cold-Start Augmentation**}; appendix design Table 10 lists {…, **Mask Input**} instead of Cold-Start Augmentation. One variant has results without a design row; the other has a design row without results. Align them.
- **Mature gate value.** Text and conclusion say mature ḡ=0.85 (age>2 yr); Fig. `gate_by_age` caption says "→0.98 (mature)." Clarify that 0.98 is the oldest bucket and 0.85 the >2-yr average, or unify.
- **Positive fraction.** §Data says 5.9%; Table 8 says 5.8% (63,927/1,105,292 = 5.78%, so 5.8% is correct); intro rounds to "6%." Harmonize to 5.8%.
- **AdamW citation.** Line 311 cites `zhou2024towards` for AdamW; it's Loshchilov & Hutter (2019). Wrong reference.
- **Figure filenames with spaces** (`fig1_main_comparison (1).pdf`, `figC_attention_analysis (2).png`) — these break on some TeX builds; rename before camera-ready.
- Author block still has `Firstname5…` placeholders (lines 89–94).

**One substantive point, not bookkeeping.** The CS-Pos primary metric rests on "8.3% of test observations" in the 14-day window (≈ a few hundred positive station-hours after the 5.8% positive rate), but the paper never states *how many distinct stations* open inside the test window — which is the real unit of independence here. Given the honest "limited samples at 180–365d" and the failure-case paragraph, I'd add the count of cold-start test stations and a bootstrap CI on CS-Pos to Table 1. It converts the headline from "could be a handful of stations" to a defensible interval, and it's the single thing most likely to come up in review. (Relatedly, a reviewer may ask why the spatial pathway aggregates only the last latent state `h_{t-1}` rather than neighbor *histories* — worth one preemptive sentence.)

Happy to walk through it like we're at a whiteboard. I'll build it up from the problem, and keep the jargon out.

**The one-sentence version:** This project builds an AI model that predicts how busy EV charging stations will be each hour — and its special trick is making good predictions for *brand-new* stations that have almost no history yet.

**Step 1 — What are we trying to predict?**
For each charging station, in each hour, how many charging sessions will start? Knowing this matters to three groups: the power grid (so it can handle the load), the charging companies (for pricing and staffing), and city planners (deciding where to build next). The raw data is a big list of charging sessions — when each one started, how much energy, which station, where it is — and we boil it down to "station *i*, hour *t*, this many sessions."

**Step 2 — The hard part: new stations.**
New charging stations get built constantly. A station that opened yesterday has no track record, so how do you predict its demand? This is the **cold-start problem**, and it's the heart of the paper. Think of a brand-new restaurant with zero reviews: you can't judge it from its own history, so you guess based on *similar restaurants nearby*. Most existing AI models quietly assume every station already has years of data, so they fall apart exactly where a good prediction is most useful — the moment a station opens and someone's deciding whether to build more.

**Step 3 — Two annoying things about the data.**
First, **almost everything is zero**. About 94% of station-hours have no charging at all — charging is bursty and rare. A lazy model could just say "zero, always" and be right 94% of the time, while being completely useless. It's like predicting rain in a desert: "no rain" is almost always correct but tells you nothing about the rare storm you actually care about.
Second, **"empty" has two meanings**. Before a station opens, there's simply no data (truly missing). After it opens, an empty hour is a *real* zero (the station existed, nobody charged). The project carefully tags every hour with an "observation mask" so the model never confuses "didn't exist yet" with "existed but quiet." Getting this wrong would poison everything.

**Step 4 — The key idea: let the strategy depend on a station's age.**
Here's the insight the whole model is built around. A young station with no history should **lean on its neighbors** — borrow patterns from nearby, established stations. An old station with years of its own data should **trust itself** — it already knows its own rhythms (morning commuters, weekend dips). So the model should *smoothly slide* from "rely on neighbors" to "rely on yourself" as a station gets older. It's like training wheels: new riders depend on the support; experienced riders balance on their own.

**Step 5 — The model, in three pieces (this is "TA-GNN").**
The model runs two "pathways" at once and then blends them:
- A **temporal pathway** (a sequence model called a GRU) reads the station's *own* recent history.
- A **spatial pathway** (graph attention) looks at *other* stations and decides which ones are worth listening to.
Then comes the star ingredient: an **age gate**, a dial that depends on age. Young station → dial turns toward neighbors; old station → dial turns toward its own history. It's "monotonic," meaning as age increases the dial only ever moves one way (toward self-reliance) and never flip-flops. The model *learns* where the 50/50 point is — it landed at roughly 4 months of age.

**Step 6 — Two smaller but clever touches.**
First, **directional attention**: when a new station looks around for help, it's nudged to pay attention to *older, established* stations (which have useful patterns) and to ignore other *new* stations (which have nothing to teach). Like an apprentice learning from master craftsmen, not from fellow apprentices. It also refuses to peek at stations that haven't opened yet — no cheating by looking into the future.
Second, the **two-question trick** (the "hurdle" head): instead of predicting the number directly, the model asks two separate questions — "*Will anything happen this hour?*" (a yes/no chance) and "*If it does, how much?*" (the amount) — then multiplies them. This is like a doctor first asking "are you sick at all?" before "how sick?" Splitting it keeps the rare "something happened" cases from getting drowned out by the ocean of zeros.

**Step 7 — How it's trained.**
A few practical moves: the model is told to count each rare "charging happened" event ~16× more heavily so it doesn't ignore them; during training it sometimes *pretends an old station is brand-new* (wiping its history) so it gets practice on the hard case; and it stops training at the point where it's best specifically at the *new-station* task, not the easy overall task. It's also tested fairly: train on the earlier time period, test on the later one, so it's genuinely predicting the future rather than memorizing.

**Step 8 — What they found.**
On the new-station metric, TA-GNN beats every comparison model — about **28% lower error** than the next best. The surprising twist: plain graph models actually did *worse* than a simple no-graph model on new stations, because naively averaging a bunch of neighbors *dilutes* the tiny bit of signal you have. TA-GNN avoids that by being selective (the gate + directional attention). And when they cracked the model open, it had learned exactly the intended behavior on its own: new stations put about **65% of their weight on neighbors**, old stations about **85% on their own history**, and new stations' attention flowed toward the 1–2-year-old "veteran" stations. That last part is the satisfying bit — the model wasn't told to do this; it discovered the sensible strategy from the data.

So the takeaway: the contribution isn't just "another forecasting model," it's a clean way to handle the *new-node* problem in any growing network — phrased here for EV charging, but the same idea would apply to newly added sensors, new bike-share docks, or new stores.

Great instinct — that's exactly the kind of number you should never take on faith. There are three ways to check it, from "10 seconds with a calculator" to "2 minutes of code that settles it for good." I'll go in order, and I'll flag the one trap that makes people get a wildly wrong answer.

**Check 1 — Does the paper's own number even add up? (10 seconds)**

The paper reports three numbers (Table 8): 1,105,292 observed station-hours, 63,927 of them positive, 1,041,365 zero. First just confirm the parts equal the whole:

63,927 + 1,041,365 = 1,105,292 ✓ — and 1,041,365 ÷ 1,105,292 = **94.2%**.

So the 94% is at least *self-consistent* — nobody fat-fingered the percentage. That's necessary but not sufficient; the inputs themselves could still be wrong.

**Check 2 — Does 94% square with how many sessions there are? (back-of-envelope)**

There are 82,950 charging sessions total. Picture the most extreme case where no two sessions ever land in the same station-hour — then you'd have at most 82,950 non-zero hours, i.e. 82,950 ÷ 1,105,292 = **7.5%** non-zero. In reality sessions cluster (a busy station gets several in one hour), so the true non-zero rate has to be *below* 7.5%. The paper's 5.8% sits just under that ceiling — plausible. ✓

A useful by-product: 82,950 sessions ÷ 63,927 busy hours ≈ **1.3 sessions per busy hour**, which matches the reported median of 1.0 with a right skew. (Side note: the paper separately claims a *mean* positive demand of 1.89, which would imply ~120,000 sessions, not 82,950 — so *that* number is the one that doesn't reconcile, not the 94%. Worth confirming when you run Check 3.)

**Check 3 — Recompute it directly from the data (definitive, ~2 min)**

This is the real double-check. Load the processed tensor and count:

```python
import torch
data = torch.load('data/processed/tensors/data_v4.pt', weights_only=False)
Y, M = data['Y'], data['M']          # Y = hourly session counts, M = observation mask

observed   = (M == 1)                 # station was OPEN and hour is real
n_obs      = observed.sum().item()
n_positive = ((Y > 0) & observed).sum().item()
n_zero     = ((Y == 0) & observed).sum().item()

print(f"Observed station-hours: {n_obs:,}")
print(f"Zero:     {n_zero:,} ({100*n_zero/n_obs:.2f}%)")
print(f"Positive: {n_positive:,} ({100*n_positive/n_obs:.2f}%)")
print(f"Zero:positive ratio = {n_zero/n_positive:.2f} : 1")
print(f"Total sessions = {Y[observed].sum().item():,.0f}")
print(f"Mean over busy hours = {Y[(Y>0)&observed].float().mean():.2f}")
```

If the paper is right, this prints ~94.2% zeros, a 16.3:1 ratio, ~82,950 sessions, and a mean around 1.3. (You don't even strictly need to write this — `preprocess_v4.py` already prints "Hours with zero demand but observed" and "Ratio zeros/positive" at the end of its run, so you can just rerun preprocessing or check its log.)

**The trap — and why the mask is the whole ballgame**

Notice every count above is filtered by `observed` (`M == 1`). That's not optional. Here's what happens if you forget it.

The full grid is 28,758 hours × 118 stations = 3,393,444 cells, but only 1,105,292 are observed. The other ~2.29 million cells are *before each station opened* — that's missing data, not zero demand. If you lazily counted "any cell where Y isn't positive" as a zero, you'd get (3,393,444 − 63,927) ÷ 3,393,444 = **98.1%**, not 94%. That inflated number would be wrong — it's secretly mostly "this station didn't exist yet," which has nothing to do with charging being rare.

So the honest claim is precise: **of the hours when a station was actually open, 94% had no charging.** The denominator is the 1.1M open hours, never the full 3.4M grid. That distinction — "didn't exist yet" versus "existed but quiet" — is exactly the data-cleaning step the paper makes a point of, and it's the thing to be most careful about when you verify the number yourself.

import pandas as pd, re

# Strip trailing port/connector suffixes like  ~2  ~4  -2  _1  from the name
def base_site(name):
    s = str(name)
    s = re.sub(r'[\s_~\-]*\d+$', '', s)         # drop trailing port number
    s = re.sub(r'[\s,]+$', '', s)

Two different questions hiding in there — "*should* we sum ports?" (a modeling-correctness question) and "*what's actually broken?*" (a bug-hunt). The first one reframes the second, so let me take it first.

## Is it correct to sum all ports of one station?

**Yes — for what this project predicts, summing ports up to the physical site is the correct and standard choice.** The target here is *arrivals/demand at a location* (how many charging sessions start at this place this hour). That quantity is inherently site-level: a driver picks a *site*, the grid sees the *site's* total load, and a planner sites a *location*, not a plug. The graph is geographic (locations), so co-located plugs are just redundant copies of one node. And summing reduces the artificial sparsity — one lonely plug is idle most hours by construction, which is part of why you're seeing 94% zeros.

The only times you would *not* sum: if you were predicting **per-plug occupancy/availability** ("is a stall free right now"), or if connector types are so different you want them modeled separately — in which case you'd split by *type* (CCS vs CHAdeMO), not by individual plug.

So summing isn't the bug. **The bug is that the pipeline doesn't sum consistently.** It effectively sums for Electric Era and Kempower (whose IDs are site-level) but *splits every plug into its own node* for ChargePoint, ZEFNET, and EV Connect (whose IDs are plug-level). That's how you got 118 nodes for 94 real sites, with `K0024972A` becoming 6 separate "stations." You have a mix of summed and un-summed — that's the inconsistency to fix.

## What's actually wrong with the processing

In rough priority order:

**1. Inconsistent node granularity — the node key is a raw name string (confirmed bug).** Each provider derives `station_id` from a name/address (lines 269, 313, etc.). For ZEFNET/ChargePoint/EVConnect that name *includes a port suffix* (`~2`, `Station 2`), so plugs become separate nodes; for Electric Era/Kempower it's site-level. Fix: define one physical-site key for all five providers (strip port suffixes; for ChargePoint, confirm with lat/lon; for ZEFNET/Kempower the serial identifies the unit) and aggregate all plugs within a site.

**2. `num_evses` is computed wrong as a direct consequence (confirmed bug).** It's `nunique(evse_id)` *per station_id* — but `station_id` is already plug-level for most providers, so it returns ≈1 for 111 of 118 nodes. The intended feature ("ports at this site") is not what's stored; the model is being fed a near-constant. After re-aggregation it becomes meaningful (and *correct* ports-per-site).

**3. The mask never closes — dead stations stay "open and idle" forever (suspected — needs checking).** The mask sets M=1 from a station's first session to the *end of the whole grid* (line 496). Opening is estimated as the first session, but there's no matching "close." So if a station was decommissioned or stopped reporting in 2023, every hour from then to Nov 2025 is still counted as an *observed zero*. That would inflate the 94% and corrupt the very zeros-vs-missing distinction the paper leans on. Checkable below.

**4. ChargePoint timestamp resolution (suspected — needs checking).** `process_chargepoint` parses `Start Date` with no separate time column. If that field is date-only, then for 65% of your sessions every event lands at midnight and the hour-of-day feature is garbage. I don't know yet — but it's cheap to verify and would be a serious bug if true.

**5. Known design limitations (not bugs, but worth stating).** Only ChargePoint has coordinates, so the *distance prior* is ChargePoint-only and the other 21 nodes have no spatial neighbors except through learned attention. The DC-fast filter is only applied to ChargePoint (the rest are assumed DCFC). All timestamps are forced to US/Eastern, phase-shifting non-Eastern sites. These are defensible, but they're assumptions, not facts.

Let me confirm #3 and #4 before we touch any code — facts first. Run this:

Before I write `preprocess_v5.py`, there's exactly one decision only you can make, because it changes the site key — **for ZEFNET, is a "site" the serial unit or the connector?** Your data has `SM-K0024972A` split into `~1` through `~6`. Two readings:

- `K0024972A` is **one physical charging unit** and `~1…~6` are its connectors → collapse all 6 into one node (gives ~94 sites).
- `K0024972A~1` and `~2` are **physically separate pedestals** that happen to share a serial prefix → keep them separate.

The suffix pattern (`~N`) almost always means connectors on one unit, which is why I'd collapse — but you know this hardware and I don't. This one check will show you the demand patterns side by side so you can decide:

```bash
python3 - << 'EOF'
import pandas as pd, torch, numpy as np
d = torch.load('data/processed/tensors/data_v4.pt', weights_only=False)
m = pd.read_csv('data/processed/unified/station_metadata_v4.csv')
Y, ti = d['Y'].numpy(), pd.to_datetime(d['time_index'])
ids = list(m['station_id'])

# Show the 6 ZEFNET connectors of SM-K0024972A: do they share an opening date
# and overlap in time? (siblings on one unit) or tile different periods?
grp = m[m['station_name'].str.contains('K0024972A', case=False, na=False)]
print("ZEFNET SM-K0024972A family:")
print(grp[['station_name','open_time','last_time','total_sessions','num_evses']].to_string(index=False))

# Hours where >1 of these connectors are active simultaneously
cols = [ids.index(s) for s in grp['station_id'] if s in ids]
sub = Y[:, cols]
both_active = (sub > 0).sum(axis=1)
print(f"\nHours with >=2 connectors active at once: {(both_active>=2).sum():,}")
print("  (many simultaneous-active hours => true sibling connectors => collapse them)")
print("  (near-zero overlap => maybe separate pedestals tiling time => keep separate)")
EOF
```

If those 6 connectors open around the same time and frequently run simultaneously, they're one unit → collapse. If they barely overlap (one stops when the next starts), they might be sequential replacements and you'd treat them differently.

- **sums all plugs per site** into one demand series,
- recomputes **`num_ports`** and **`num_port_types`** (CCS/CHAdeMO) as real site features,
- adds the **mask close rule** (end mask N days after last session) to mop up the 1.4%,
- and prints a **before/after diff** (N: 118→~94, the new zero-rate, sessions conserved as a checksum) so you can see exactly what moved and confirm nothing leaked.

That's a clear answer, and it points to **collapse** — these six are connectors on one physical unit, not separate pedestals. Here's how I read the evidence:

- **They open within an 8-day window** (Sep 18 – Oct 1, 2024) and all run until Nov 2025. Separate pedestals installed over a year of expansion wouldn't cluster like that; six connectors energized together at one commissioning do.
- **They overlap in time, not tile.** The "sequential replacement" hypothesis predicts one dies as the next is born (near-zero simultaneous activity). You have 60 hours with ≥2 active at once — small in absolute terms, but that's expected: at ~5.8% positive rate, the chance of two specific low-traffic connectors both firing in the same hour is tiny, so 60 co-active hours is plenty to confirm they coexist rather than replace each other.
- **The shared serial** `SM-K0024972A` with `~1…~6` connector suffixes is exactly the ZEFNET/Kempower naming convention for one unit's plugs.

One thing the overlap number *does* tell you, and it matters for the modeling story: even on a 6-connector unit, simultaneous use is rare (60 hours over a year). So when you sum them, you won't get a smooth busy series — you'll get the **sum of six sparse series**, which is denser than any single plug but still zero most hours. That's fine and correct; just don't expect collapsing to dramatically cut the 94%. It'll move it a little, not transform it. Demand is genuinely sparse at the site level too.

So the rule for `preprocess_v5.py` is settled: **collapse on the serial-without-suffix** (`SM-K0024972A`, `DT-K0024977A`, etc.) for ZEFNET and Kempower, and on the suffix-stripped name (confirmed by coordinates where present) for ChargePoint. Sum all connectors per site.

**2. When connectors at a site disagree on metadata, what wins?** Within `SM-K0024972A`, the connectors have different open dates (Sep 18 vs Oct 1) and could differ on coordinates/port type. The aggregation rules I'll use — tell me if you want any changed:
- **open_time** = **earliest** connector (the site opened when its first plug went live → Sep 18). This is the right choice for cold-start: the *site* isn't "new" just because plug ~2 came online two weeks later.
- **last_time** = latest connector.
- **demand** = hourly sum across connectors.
- **num_ports** = count of connectors; **num_port_types** = distinct CCS/CHAdeMO.
- **coordinates** = first non-null among connectors.
- **provider** = the shared one (all six are ZEFNET, so no conflict).

That `open_time = earliest` choice is the one with real consequences — it's what makes the collapsed site stop looking like a "new station" every time a port is added, which is precisely the contamination you want gone. I'm fairly confident it's correct, but flag it if your hardware reality differs (e.g., if plugs are sometimes added to a site months later as a true capacity expansion you'd want modeled as a change).

Run the Kempower check, confirm the `open_time = earliest` rule, and then I'll write the full `preprocess_v5.py` — one site key across all five providers, summed connectors, real port features, the mask close rule for that 1.4% tail, and a before/after printout with a **session-count checksum** (total sessions must stay 82,950 — if collapsing changes that number, something's wrong and we'll see it immediately).

Perfect — that's the last piece of reconnaissance, and it tells us the collapse rule has to be **provider-aware**, not one-size-fits-all:

- **ZEFNET: 14 → 3** (heavy port-splitting; collapse on serial)

Total lands at **3 + 84 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 94 sites**, matching the independent collapse from two turns ago. The fact that two different methods both give 94 is a good consistency signal.

The Kempower result is exactly why I made you run that check: it's already aggregated (`K0024986A` is one node covering its connectors), so if I'd blindly applied the suffix-strip to everything I'd have been fine there — but the real trap is the *opposite*. Stripping trailing digits is dangerous for any provider whose site names legitimately *end in a number* (a street address like "...Highway 27", a "Store #5"). For Kempower it happens to be a no-op, but I won't trust the regex globally. The safe construction is: **strip the `~N` connector suffix only** (that token is unambiguous — it only ever means a connector), and for ChargePoint additionally use coordinates to confirm a merge before collapsing names. That avoids accidentally gluing together two genuinely different sites that just share a name prefix.

Let me read the top of the file.Now I have the full pipeline and the coordinate situation is clear: **ChargePoint has real lat/lon (line 151–152); the other four providers are NaN.** That's the key that makes a safe merge possible — I can verify ChargePoint merges geographically (so a regex that accidentally glues "Highway 27" and "Highway 41" gets caught), while ZEFNET/Kempower use their unambiguous `~N`/serial pattern.

Here's the design I'll implement, then the code:

- **Site key, provider-aware:** strip the `~N` connector tag for ZEFNET; strip the trailing connector number (and stray `(LM)`) for ChargePoint; leave Kempower / Electric Era / EV Connect untouched (already site-level).
- **Safety net:** for ChargePoint (has coords), flag any site whose merged connectors sit >1 km apart — a bad merge reveals itself instead of silently corrupting the graph.
- **Real port features:** `num_ports = max(distinct connectors, distinct EVSE ids)` per site (handles both the name-encoded ZEFNET case and the evse-encoded Kempower case), plus `num_port_types` (CCS/CHAdeMO).
- **open_time = earliest connector** (so adding a plug doesn't make a known site look "new" — kills the contamination at the source), `last_time` = latest, demand = hourly **sum** across connectors.
- **Mask close rule** (conservative 90-day grace) to mop up the 1.4% trailing zeros.
- **Checksum:** total sessions must stay 82,950 after collapsing — printed loudly. Writes to `*_v5` files; **nothing v4 is overwritten.**Done. `preprocess_v5.py` is ready to run on your server — I can't run it here since the raw Excel lives on your machine, but it's heavily instrumented so the printout will tell you immediately if anything's off.

**What it does**, and why each piece is there:

The provider parsing is copied verbatim from v4 — I changed *nothing* about how sessions/timestamps are read, since we confirmed those are correct. The only new logic is what happens *after* parsing:

1. **One physical-site key for all five providers.** ZEFNET loses its `~N` connector tag; ChargePoint loses a trailing connector number (and stray `(LM)`); Kempower/Electric Era/EV Connect are left alone because they're already site-level. The original plug id is kept as `connector_id` so nothing is lost and you can audit every merge.

2. **Coordinate guard on ChargePoint merges.** Before merging, it checks that a site's connectors sit within 1 km of each other (ChargePoint is the only provider with coords). If a name-regex ever tried to glue two genuinely different addresses, it prints `! NOT merging …` and keeps them separate. This is the safety net that makes the regex trustworthy.

3. **Real port features.** `num_ports = max(distinct connectors, distinct EVSE ids)` — this is the fix for v4's broken `num_evses` (which was ≈1 for 111/118). It correctly gets 6 for ZEFNET's `K0024972A` and 4 for Kempower's multi-connector sites. Also adds `num_port_types`.

4. **`open_time` = earliest connector** — the fix that stops a known site from looking "new" when a plug is added, which is exactly the cold-start contamination we checked for.

5. **Mask close rule** (90-day grace) to trim that 1.4% of trailing zeros from churned stations. Set `MASK_CLOSE_DAYS = None` at the top if you want exact v4 mask behavior.

6. **A loud checksum:** total sessions in `Y` must equal sessions fed in. If collapsing ever dropped or duplicated a session, you'll see `FAIL ✗`.

"""
EV_GNN Data Preprocessing Pipeline v5

FIXES from v4:
  (BUG) Node granularity was inconsistent across providers:
        - ChargePoint / ZEFNET / EVConnect used PLUG-level ids  -> ports split into separate "stations"
        - ElectricEra / Kempower used SITE-level ids             -> ports already aggregated
        Result: 118 "stations" for ~94 physical sites (e.g. ZEFNET K0024972A = 6 nodes).

  v5 collapses connectors -> ONE physical site per location, consistently for all 5 providers:
        - demand is SUMMED across a site's connectors (correct site-level target)
        - num_ports / num_port_types become real per-site features (v4's num_evses was ~1 for 111/118)
        - open_time = EARLIEST connector (so adding a plug does NOT make a site look "new")
        - ChargePoint merges are coordinate-verified (>1km apart => flagged, NOT merged)

  Minor: optional mask "close" rule trims observed-zeros that trail a station's last session
         by more than MASK_CLOSE_DAYS (v4 kept churned stations "open" to the grid end forever).

Outputs are written to *_v5 files. NOTHING from v4 is overwritten.

Usage:
    export EV_GNN_ROOT=/home/jovyan/GNN
    python preprocess_v5.py
"""
